articles.title: The signs were there: inside experimentation’s final months
articles.standfirst: Months of frank warnings about ownership, discoverability and organisational inaction culminate in a quietly cancelled project and an unofficial Friday wind-down.

blocks.alt: The signs were there: inside experimentation’s final months

runs.text: The BBC experimentation assignment has ended with a cancellation that, in retrospect, seems less like a sudden shock than the logical conclusion of months of warnings about a process struggling to justify itself.

For UX designer Sam Smith, Friday 9 October was the moment the subtext became text. After months spent investigating the BBC's experimentation process, interviewing colleagues and mapping practical difficulties across its lifecycle, the work was being wound down. The warning signs had been there in meeting after meeting.
The process everyone could describe, but nobody could quite make work
The programme promised a more accessible, repeatable route from an idea to a test and then to a decision. The research instead found friction at almost every hand-off. Work was mapped across
Ideate, Plan, Build, Test, Decide and Learn
, with recurring questions about ownership, getting hold of the right expertise, discoverability of existing experiments and learning, and knowing what was actually expected of teams.

These were not simply cosmetic UX problems. If colleagues struggle to discover what has already been tried, understand who can unblock them or navigate the process without chasing individuals, then a supposed self-service capability is not meaningfully self-service. A process diagram cannot substitute for empowered people, decisions and organisational commitment.

The July discussions around continuous discovery showed how the work often happened outside any tidy, linear experimentation model. September conversations with Divya, Dan and Bernie sharpened the distinction between a presentable process and the actual conditions required to make it usable. The challenge was not a lack of sticky notes, themes or polished artefacts. It was whether anyone could act on the diagnosis.
A project pushed forward for its own sake

By September, Smith was privately questioning whether the group was being asked to keep going largely because work had already begun. Bernie, by his account, recognised the problems but was trying to remain pragmatic. Smith feared that producing something visually convincing could amount to dressing up deeper organisational dysfunction as design progress.

The bluntest criticism was not that experimentation was a bad idea. It was that the operating environment had failed to support the ambition. Access to expertise, clarity of roles, practical capacity and clear routes to decisions needed to exist before a polished experience could deliver its promised value. Otherwise the work risked becoming documentation of a broken process rather than a means of changing it.
There is an important distinction here: those assessments draw on Smith's recollections and reflections about the meetings, not a verified verbatim transcript of every remark.
“Don't need to flog a dead horse”

The ending arrived with startling informality. At 09:49 on Friday, Bernie Martin messaged: “Um maybe lets chill on this work today? Dont need to flog a dead horse if no one is looking at it! What do ya think?”

Smith agreed, suggesting some polishing on Monday, and acknowledged that he had seen the outcome coming but found its confirmation strange. Bernie replied that it felt “a bit odd” and recalled that Gruff had been “shifty” when shown the team's latest work on Wednesday. In hindsight, she felt, that interaction made more sense.

The exchange then became a farewell. “Very fun! Thanks for being an awesome work buddy and PP guru!” Bernie wrote. The pair exchanged affectionate goodbyes, with Smith suggesting their paths would cross again.
Bernie's immediate instinct was, essentially, to sack off the day rather than perform productivity for an audience that had vanished. In the language of Smith's schooldays, it felt like
“dogging it”

. Dan had not explicitly assigned replacement work, and was himself off that day. Smith interpreted the silence as an unspoken understanding to leave it alone; it was not an expressly agreed day off or formal permission to stop working.
The cost of the warning signs

It would be easy to call the research wasted. That would let the more important failure disappear. The team had surfaced genuine barriers and put names to problems people had been living with. What remained missing was a structure willing and able to do something consequential with those findings.

The cancellation leaves an uncomfortable question: how much evidence of a dysfunctional process must an organisation collect before it decides whether to fix that process, or stop asking designers to make it look functional?

articles.title: SwS heads to London for SNL UK dress rehearsal
articles.standfirst: London visit confirmed for a Saturday Night Live UK dress rehearsal as Danny Dyer prepares to host with musical guest Sasha Keable.

blocks.alt: SwS heads to London for SNL UK dress rehearsal

runs.text: Government for SwS has confirmed plans to travel to London for a dress rehearsal of
Saturday Night Live UK
, ahead of its broadcast on Saturday 10 October 2026. An RSVP invitation was received from NBCUniversal on 29 September, providing the basis for attendance arrangements.

The visit forms part of a short trip from Glasgow to London between Friday 9 and Sunday 11 October. It will provide an opportunity to experience a major live television comedy production from inside the studio, rather than through the finished television broadcast.
Sky has announced that actor Danny Dyer will host the 10 October episode, with singer-songwriter Sasha Keable appearing as musical guest. Dyer is known for roles in
EastEnders
Rivals
and
Mr Big Stuff
. The episode is part of the programme's second series, which began in September 2026.
Saturday Night Live UK

is the British adaptation of NBC's long-running American sketch comedy show. The format brings together a rotating celebrity host, an ensemble of comedians, live musical performances and topical sketches. It also includes a British version of
Weekend Update
, the satirical news segment established by the original series.

The British production launched on Sky and NOW on 21 March 2026 with Tina Fey hosting and Wet Leg as musical guest. Later hosts included Jamie Dornan and Riz Ahmed. Following its initial run, Sky commissioned a second series of 12 additional episodes, scheduled across autumn 2026 and early 2027.

For the October run, Sky has also confirmed James Norton and The Streets for 17 October, followed by Cynthia Erivo and Blossoms on 24 October. The programme is produced in London by Universal Television Alternative Studio's UK production team and Broadway Video for Sky and NOW, with Lorne Michaels among its executive producers.

The rehearsal is distinct from the televised programme. Dress rehearsals allow the production to run material with an audience before the final live broadcast and are part of the process of preparing a fast-moving weekly comedy show. The final combination of sketches and their performance may differ from what is seen during rehearsal.

The NBCUniversal email is headed “SNL UK DRESS TICKET RSVP” and links to an RSVP form. It establishes that the invitation was issued, but does not specify a final admission time or provide a complete entry confirmation within the message itself. Attendance will therefore remain subject to the arrangements communicated by the production.
The London visit is scheduled to conclude on Sunday 11 October. An account of the experience may follow once the trip has taken place.

Sky, series-two announcement
; NBCUniversal RSVP email, 29 September 2026.

articles.title: What went wrong with experimentation?
articles.standfirst: An examination of why months of BBC experimentation discovery ended in a pause, and what the project revealed about organisational change.

runs.text: On 9 October 2026, work on a BBC experimentation enablement assignment was paused. The decision followed months of research into how digital product teams conceive, deliver and learn from experiments. Why did a substantial discovery effort reach this point without a corresponding implemented improvement?

The available evidence suggests not one spectacular failure but a familiar organisational mismatch: a design investigation was making problems visible faster than the surrounding programme could agree what to do about them. That is an interpretation of the project experience, not a confirmed statement of the BBC's reasons for pausing the work.
The problem was bigger than a process map

UX designer Sam Smith joined the experimentation team in June after working on Account and design systems. Exposure to live experiments, including local trending content and iPlayer playback and recommendation behaviours, established the practical terrain.

Research then examined six phases of experimentation: IDEATE, PLAN, BUILD, TEST, DECIDE and LEARN. Interviews and synthesis involving approximately a dozen participants exposed how much activity depended on relationships and work outside those formal stages.

The resulting heatmap, qualitative synthesis and prototype Experiment Sticky Extractor represented concrete research outputs. But describing where friction exists does not automatically establish who has the mandate, resources or appetite to remove it.
Five tensions that emerged
1. Ownership was fragmented.

Research and stakeholder conversations repeatedly returned to the need to find the right people and expertise at the right moment. This points to cross-team dependencies that a UX artefact cannot fix by itself.
2. The official journey was incomplete.

Continuous discovery, informal coordination and prerequisite decisions did not always fit neatly into the six-stage model. Improving a published process would not necessarily improve the real experience.
3. Discoverability was a symptom, not necessarily the diagnosis.
Making tools, guidance or specialists easier to find might help, but it would not resolve unavailable capacity, ambiguous decision rights or conflicting priorities.
4. Agreement on an output risked overtaking agreement on an outcome.

September discussions raised concern about producing something tangible without sufficiently resolving the purpose, scope or conditions for success. This was a design judgement emerging from the work, not an allegation of bad faith by colleagues.
5. Organisational timing mattered.

Earlier experimentation opportunity discussions had already been paused pending second-half planning clarity. The later winding down of this particular assignment should not be conflated with cancellation of experimentation across the BBC.
Explore the project's journey
Select a milestone in the interactive timeline below. It distinguishes research, deliverables, points of friction and decisions, and includes approximate dates where needed.
What might have changed the outcome?

A narrower agreed problem statement, a named accountable owner, explicit decision-making authority and a small measurable pilot could have offered a firmer bridge between discovery and delivery. These are retrospective hypotheses, not proof that an alternative route would have survived changing programme priorities.
The project also illustrates a limit of design-led transformation: a good map can identify systemic problems, but it cannot create the organisational conditions required to address them.

There is no established evidence here that the BBC's experimentation capability as a whole failed, or that particular individuals caused the pause. The supported conclusion is narrower: this piece of UX work gathered and structured useful evidence, but ended before an improvement was implemented and evaluated.

For Smith, the lasting work includes the research model, synthesis, clearer opportunity areas and experience of navigating ambiguity. For the programme, the unanswered question is whether that understanding will eventually be translated into a change that teams can feel and measure.

articles.title: Ramsden’s data team DISBANDED following experimentation dead-end
articles.standfirst: A BBC experimentation enablement assignment is paused after months of research, process mapping and stakeholder engagement.

runs.text: BBC Scotland's headquarters at Pacific Quay, Glasgow. Photograph: John Allan / Geograph,
CC BY-SA 2.0
Original image
. No alterations.
[SWS alt: Exterior of BBC Scotland's headquarters beside the River Clyde in Glasgow.]

Work on an experimentation enablement project involving BBC UX designer Sam Smith has been paused, bringing an unexpectedly abrupt end to several months of discovery, stakeholder engagement and research synthesis.

The change became clear on Friday 9 October, as the immediate need for further work on the current project fell away. Some smaller outstanding activities may remain, but the main body of work is no longer the immediate priority.
It marks a change of direction for a project that had increasingly concentrated on how experimentation happens across the BBC, rather than on the design of any single experiment.
From live experiments to a wider problem
Smith joined the experimentation team in June 2026, following earlier work in the BBC's Account design team and design systems.

The initial period involved exposure to product experiments, including local trending content, iPlayer recommendations and autoplay behaviours. That provided practical insight into the dependencies involved in planning, building, measuring and interpreting changes to digital products.

The work then broadened into a discovery exercise examining the processes and relationships that make experimentation possible. Interviews and stakeholder discussions highlighted the experiences of colleagues working across different parts of that journey.

Evidence was organised against six phases: IDEATE, PLAN, BUILD, TEST, DECIDE and LEARN. Alongside the formal stages, the research considered activity outside the process, including continuous discovery and the need for specialist support.

By September, a research heatmap had been assembled from material involving approximately a dozen participants. Findings were grouped around process steps, people, tools and blockers, allowing recurring sources of friction to be considered together.
A small prototype, the Experiment Sticky Extractor, was also developed to support the handling and synthesis of qualitative research evidence.
Questions of ownership and direction
As the work progressed, attention moved from documenting individual problems towards understanding the conditions behind them.
Themes included access to the right expertise at the right time, discoverability, handovers, unclear ownership and differences between formal processes and everyday practice.
Discussions in September also exposed uncertainty about the scope of potential improvements and what could realistically be achieved without wider organisational alignment.
This became a central tension in the project: identifying opportunities through research is not the same as securing the agreement, capacity and ownership needed to act on them.
In early October, efforts were still under way to refine the research themes into clearer statements of need, distinguishing overlapping issues and preserving the evidence behind them.
A pause, not a completed transformation

The latest change means the work has not reached a conventional delivery conclusion. There is no claim that the research led to a new operating model or measurable improvement in experimentation performance.
It has, however, produced a structured account of the experimentation experience, a body of synthesised research and clearer language for several organisational challenges.
For Smith, the project also represents experience in service-level thinking, managing ambiguity, challenging assumptions and working through stakeholder complexity.
The immediate next step is a transition away from the current experimentation assignment, with any remaining handover or smaller tasks to be settled as required.

The broader question of how the BBC improves experimentation remains separate from the status of this particular piece of UX work. For now, the project closes its most active chapter with the findings established, but the longer-term response unresolved.

SWS.GOV
has completed its migration from Craft to Notion, moving the site’s article publishing system onto a new backend while a series of smaller homepage and News improvements have also gone live.

The Notion migration is the largest of today’s changes. Work announced earlier this week to move News and Press Office content away from Craft has now been completed, making Notion the main content management system for
SWS.GOV
. The change provides a more stable base for publishing and brings article management into the same system now used by the
SWS.GOV
publishing workflow.
The migration has been completed without changing the role of
SWS.GOV
itself. Notion now acts as the source of content behind the site, while published material continues to appear through the existing
SWS.GOV
interface. Images and article metadata are accounted for as part of the new publishing structure.
A second visible change is the arrival of Glasgow Film Theatre showtimes on the homepage. Current GFT screenings can now appear directly within
SWS.GOV

, making cinema listings part of the homepage rather than requiring a separate visit to the GFT site. The feature is intended to keep useful local information close to the rest of the personal dashboard.
The Superfeed has also received further improvements. The feed combines
SWS.GOV
material with external news sources in a single ranked stream, with
SWS.GOV

stories given particular prominence while still allowing significant outside news to surface. Today’s work continues the effort to make that feed feel less like a collection of sources and more like one coherent news product.
News pages now also include a new
Picture of the Day
feature. This adds a deliberately visual element to the News experience alongside the main article feed and gives a single image more prominence within the daily layout.

Finally, cover images can now be explored in more detail through zoom and pan controls. The change is small, but it makes large photographs and artwork more useful where detail matters rather than treating the cover image as a fixed decorative element.

Together, the changes move Project Indigo further from a simple redesign towards a more complete working environment. The underlying publishing system is now more settled, while the homepage is gaining more live information and the News experience is becoming richer and more tactile.
The focus now shifts from migration work to continuing refinement of the systems already in place.

articles.title: Manger dispute sparks extraordinary dream confrontation with Sinéad O’Connor
articles.standfirst: A surreal dream involving Sinéad O’Connor, a comedy Q&A and a dispute about the Nativity ends in extraordinary confrontation.

blocks.alt: Manger dispute sparks extraordinary dream confrontation with Sinéad O’Connor

runs.text: A vivid overnight dream has placed the Government for SwS at the centre of an extraordinary confrontation involving a comedian identified as Richard Vace, the late singer Sinéad O’Connor, a former schoolmate and a dispute over the historical accuracy of the Nativity.

The incident, which took place entirely within a dream, began when the First Minister was informed that Vace was conducting a question-and-answer session at a nearby venue. The event was reportedly proving entertaining for reasons unintended by its principal speaker, who was delivering an extended denunciation of cancel culture.
Upon entering the auditorium, the First Minister discovered a substantial number of empty seats and took a place among the audience.
Political vetting precedes theological crisis
Attention soon shifted to Sinéad O’Connor, who was seated immediately ahead of the visiting party.
Before addressing the gathering, O’Connor requested a photograph for social media. However, an unidentified member of the group sought clarification of her political affiliations before consenting.
O’Connor declared herself a left-wing socialist, a position deemed satisfactory by those present. The photograph was consequently approved in principle.
The atmosphere deteriorated when the First Minister questioned the historical accuracy of the traditional account of Jesus Christ's birth in a manger.
Beth Reed, a former schoolmate remembered for her religious convictions, became visibly distressed within the dream. O’Connor also challenged the remarks.

Reed subsequently accused the First Minister of not believing in God, prompting an attempt to distinguish between scepticism about a particular religious narrative and disbelief in the existence of a deity.
The First Minister acknowledged that he did not believe in God, while maintaining that this was an entirely separate matter. The distinction failed to restore order.
Disagreement escalates
What began as a discussion of biblical interpretation developed into an extensive confrontation, with the First Minister recalling that he was actively fighting O’Connor.
The dream then took a particularly unexpected turn.

In an apparent attempt to demonstrate the biological circumstances of human reproduction, the First Minister entered into a sexual relationship with a woman identified in the dream as O’Connor's daughter.
He subsequently instructed her to inform her mother, upon the birth of their hypothetical child, that this was how children were born.
The episode represented a substantial escalation from the original disagreement, not least because the First Minister is gay.
No real-world implications identified
The Government has emphasised the distinction between involuntary dream experiences and conscious intentions or behaviour.
There is no suggestion that any of the events occurred outside the dream, nor that the individuals depicted participated in any actual confrontation.

The episode nevertheless offers a striking illustration of the sleeping mind's ability to combine familiar people, political identity, religious argument and improbable narrative developments into a single experience.
The original question of whether Jesus was born in a manger remains unresolved within the dream.
No further Q&A sessions are currently anticipated.

articles.title: The stranger who became a reminder to say yes
articles.standfirst: A chance conversation over coffee in Glasgow prompts a reflection on friendship and opportunities not taken.

blocks.alt: The stranger who became a reminder to say yes

runs.text: A brief conversation with a stranger in a busy Glasgow café has become an unexpected reminder of the value of spontaneous human connection.

On a Saturday lunchtime, Sam was waiting at Sister Midnight for two coffees: a black Americano for himself and an oat milk cappuccino for his boyfriend Adam, who was working nearby. Another customer, a young man called Ben, asked a simple question: what had he ordered?

What followed was a remarkably easy conversation. They spoke about the weather, where they lived, growing up around Glasgow, university, work and Ben's studies. Ben lived in Paisley; Sam lived in Glasgow's Southside and worked as a UX designer. Neither had arrived expecting to meet anyone new.

The conversation was not dramatic. Its significance lay in how natural it felt. Within minutes, the usual effort of talking to a stranger seemed to disappear. Each question led to another. There was an immediate sense of being on a similar wavelength.
Eventually the coffees were ready. They exchanged names and parted with the familiar promise, 'I'll see you around.' No social media details were exchanged.
The missed connection
After spending time with Adam, Sam walked past the café again on his way to meet his parents. He hoped Ben might still be there, giving him a second opportunity to ask for his Instagram. He wasn't.

There was an element of attraction, too. Sam was struck by Ben's beautiful blue eyes and wondered whether the friendly exchange might also have contained a little flirting. But the stranger's sexuality and intentions remain unknown, and the desire to reconnect was about the possibility of friendship.

That distinction matters. Sam remains committed to his relationship with Adam, with whom he openly discussed the encounter. Finding someone else attractive does not undermine a loving monogamous relationship, nor does a fleeting fantasy amount to a decision to act on it.
A lesson beyond the café

Ben has since acquired a symbolic role larger than the few minutes they spent talking. He is the stranger who may never appear again, the possible friend whose story stopped before it properly began, and the reminder that interesting people can enter ordinary days without warning.

The practical lesson is not to chase strangers or turn every pleasant interaction into a friendship campaign. It is to recognise the occasional conversation that feels unusually easy and give it somewhere to go: exchange details, suggest coffee, accept an invitation or simply ask another question.

There is a second lesson, too. Ben initiated the exchange. Without that small act of confidence, two people would have stood beside one another, collected their drinks and left without discovering any connection at all.

Perhaps the two will meet again. Perhaps they won't. Either way, the encounter has already had an effect. The next time an unexpected opportunity for connection appears, the intention is to be a little less hesitant, and perhaps, occasionally, to be the person who asks the first question.

articles.title: When DotNetBar made WinForms look like the future
articles.standfirst: The .NET component suite turned ordinary Visual Basic and C# applications into glossy, Office-inspired software and became a fixture of 2000s Windows development.

blocks.alt: When DotNetBar made WinForms look like the future

runs.text: DotNetBar belongs to a particular period of Windows software history: the years when a Visual Basic or C# application could go from looking unmistakably like a stock Windows Forms programme to something resembling Microsoft Office with a few controls dragged onto a form.

Developed by DevComponents, DotNetBar became one of the better-known third-party component suites for .NET desktop software during the 2000s. Its appeal was straightforward. Windows Forms gave developers a dependable set of native controls, but producing a heavily styled interface meant doing substantial custom drawing or relying on a specialist library. DotNetBar sold the shortcut.
The Office look arrives

The suite expanded into a large collection of replacement and extended controls, including ribbons, toolbars, docking systems, tab containers, navigation panes, buttons, text fields, calendars, sliders and DataGridView replacements.

Its visual language closely followed the Microsoft software of the period. Office 2003 and Visual Studio styling gave way to the more dramatic Office 2007 era, with gradients, rounded glossy surfaces, blue and silver colour schemes, oversized ribbon interfaces and elaborate navigation.

That was not a niche concern. In 2007, Visual Studio Magazine readers gave DotNetBar Suite a Readers Choice award in the Windows Forms UI components category. A 2008 buyer's guide listed DotNetBar for Windows Forms at $234 and the WPF edition at $299, alongside a substantial commercial market for developer interface components.
Visual Studio Magazine's 2007 awards
More than decorative buttons
It is easy to remember DotNetBar mainly for controls such as
ButtonX
, but the library was considerably broader than a skinning package.

The Windows Forms suite was advertised as a toolbox of 89 components. Its catalogue included document docking, Outlook-style navigation, tabbed interfaces, alert windows, wizard controls, custom scrollbars and styled replacements for common form components.

The ribbon was particularly significant. DevComponents later said it had released its first Windows Forms ribbon control in 2005, before the ribbon became a routine part of Microsoft's own developer tooling. When WPF emerged, the company produced a separate DotNetBar suite for that framework, including ribbon, docking and navigation components built specifically around WPF.
DotNetBar for Windows Forms
DotNetBar for WPF
A very 2000s development culture
DotNetBar also says something about how desktop software was made at the time.

Visual Studio encouraged direct manipulation. A developer could open the Windows Forms designer, drag a control onto a form, set properties in a panel, double-click it and immediately start writing event-handler code. Third-party vendors fitted neatly into that workflow by adding increasingly elaborate components to the same toolbox.
For hobbyist
VB.NET

development in particular, the effect could be dramatic. A fairly ordinary application could suddenly have an Office-style ribbon, animated panels, colour schemes and custom tabs without the developer having to build a rendering system themselves.

That aesthetic has dated, but the underlying proposition has not. Modern design systems, component libraries and UI frameworks still promise much the same thing: reusable behaviour and visual consistency packaged so product teams do not have to reinvent every interface element.
DotNetBar was simply an unusually vivid version of that idea, from an era when making a desktop app look like Office 2007 felt like making it look like the future.

articles.title: Government to consult with GP on a return to SSRIs
articles.standfirst: Telephone appointment confirmed for the afternoon of Wednesday, May 20, 2026

runs.text: Last week, we felt a stark reminder of the burdens of social anxiety. It's clear that, while we've made a tremendous amount of progress in many areas of life - from fitness to finances, from intellect to employment, we still have more to do.

As Absurdists, we firmly believe in learning from empirical evidence. We've had experience of falling down and picking ourselves back up plenty of times before. When we took power, we were deep in a physical dependence to cannabis. It wasn't easy to get out of, and despite a steadfast common consensus, we still faced numerous relapses. We learned from that experience, and now the common consensus has held for two months, our longest time without THC in half a decade. We're not going back.

This can be applied to anxiety, and mental health in a broader sense, also. The truth is – we've been here before. It's not the first time we've felt these struggles up close. We've learned to cope in many ways – and we've applied those learnings consistently throughout our daily life. One of those learnings is that sometimes, medical intervention is needed.

This Wednesday afternoon, I'll be having a conversation with our GP about our anxiety. This won't be a direct request for a return to SSRIs, but I'll discuss our past experiences and how they worked for us before. It's very possible that we'll leave the conversation with a prescription and be back taking them by the end of this week. I'm seeking to rely on the expertise of our GP – and I commit to taking their advice.
In addition to this, we're taking a number of other steps to improve our mental health. This includes, but isn't limited to:
Controlled exposure to social situations
Apple Fitness+ powered mindfulness exercises
Increased frequency at the gym, upping from twice a week to three times a week, most weeks
Daily journaling, inspired by the writing style of David Byrne's
Bicycle Diaries
Research into stoic philosophical principles

Absurdists in Government have overcome a lot. We've got more to do. I'm confident that by continuing on this holistic approach to self-improvement, we'll be better equipped to take the opportunities available to us and moving closer towards our vision of a confident, capable SwS. Thank you.

articles.title: The Case for Southsideism: Setting the Tone for AW26
articles.standfirst: Southsideism is a philosophy centred on living locally, intentionally, and in the real world. It prioritises community, health, learning, and sustainable prosperity over isolation, excess, and passive consumption. It builds on the work we've already done to implement holistic improvements – but represents a fresh push for renewed progress in AW26.

runs.text: We've reached new levels of success in the past six months
At the beginning of SS26, we set a number of goals across the four pilotis of government – and we achieved them all.

Our VO₂ Max is at an all time high, our body is more toned, our diet is more balanced and homemade - with less ultraprocessed or fast food. Cannabis is a distant memory, now fully removed from our life, which has brought benefits to our physical and mental health.

We're read 9 books so far this year, with more on the way. We've began to expand our social network and met with new friends in Glasgow, and we've been working to make this easier with the reintroduction of Citalopram and a new approach to social anxiety treatment.

Our wardrobe is more vintage and systemised, and we've acquired a sewing machine to make adjustments to our clothes. We've renewed creative output, began sharing it on Instagram, and built a name for ourselves with freelance design.

At work, we've been promoted to Midweight, dramatically increasing our income, and we've been trusted with new responsibilities and difficult challenges. We've responded well, and have received significant praise from important stakeholders.
We are clearly in a better place than we were at the start of 2026, and we've established extremely strong foundations on which we can build.
What's next

In many ways, we've been embodying elements of Southsideism for some time. As we look to strengthen areas like our place in our community, our commitment to physical and mental health, and the pursuit of knowledge and creation, it's important we do so in a way that builds on the work we've already done. Where elements of our life are working well, we'll keep going. Where there's room to improve, we'll introduce new habits and ways of thinking rooted in Southsideist ideas.
While a full set of objectives following the same format as SS26 will be issued in due course, this report serves as a tone-setting document for the philosophy that will inform their development.
Some specific areas of focus include:
Goals around a more conversational approach to dealing with people such as baristas and shopkeepers
Increased confidence around cycling and further justification of our bike
More involvement in local community groups
A limited return to the office
A push towards homeownership in the Southside, with an ambitious ten year plan for finances
Southsideism reflects our approach to life

Southsideism is ultimately a philosophy of choosing reality over abstraction. It argues that a good life is built through strong communities, meaningful relationships, good health, ethical living, continuous learning and a genuine connection to the places we inhabit. It encourages us to support the local economy, spend time outdoors, move sustainably, use technology intentionally and face discomfort as a path to growth, all while living comfortably within our means.

More than anything, Southsideism is about putting down roots. It recognises that fulfilment is rarely found in endless consumption or digital distraction, but in becoming an active participant in the life of a place. Whether through creating rather than consuming, knowing your neighbours, investing in your community or simply walking to your local café, its aim is to build a life that is healthier, more resilient and more deeply connected to the world around us.

runs.text: Our running progress has been really strong over the last few months, and our VO₂ Max has hit new heights as a result. But the truth is – we’re running too hard, too often. If we’re to improve our pace, we need to be more sensible about the way we run.
This new plan for running will ensure we have an easy aerobic base, more controlled speed work, and consistency without burnout.
New Run Routine
Monday (Run 1) – Easy Run
25 min easy to chat run (around 7:00–7:30/km effort)
Rules
If heart rate creeps up, slow down
If you feel good, stay slow (don’t get cocky!)
Wednesday (Run 2) – Intervals for Speed Work
5 min easy jog (warm up)
1 min fast (around 5:30–6:00/km effort)
2 mins very easy jog
Repeat 6 times
5 min easy jog (cool down)
Rules
Fast = controlled, not sprinting
You should finish feeling worked, not dead
Friday (Run 3) – Controlled Push for Progression
Time: 25 mins total
First 10 mins → easy (7:00/km)
Next 10 mins → steady (6:30–6:45/km)
Last 5 mins → push (as close to ~6:00/km as feels doable)
Rules
Build gradually, don’t jump straight to fast
Last 5 mins should feel tough, but not chaos
General Rules
If heart rate hits 180+ on easy runs, or you feel drained before halfway, you’re going too hard. Dial it back.

articles.title: Promotion High — But Can It Kill the Habit?
articles.standfirst: A promotion, a pay rise, and a clean slate — but can this be the moment the habit finally gets left behind?

runs.text: A pay rise. A new title. A clean slate.

For SwS, now stepping into a mid-weight UX Designer role at the BBC, this should be the moment everything clicks into place. The kind of career bump that signals not just progress at work, but a wider shift in life.
But there’s a bigger question hanging over it.
Can this be the moment the habit finally goes?
A £45K Turning Point
On paper, it’s all upside.
One of five selected from a competitive internal field. A jump to £45,000. A start date that neatly lines up with the beginning of April, and with it, the beginning of something new.
In any normal telling, that’s where the story ends.
But not here.
Because this promotion isn’t being treated as a reward. It’s being treated as leverage.
The Version Waiting to Happen
The outline of what comes next is almost cinematic.
Cycling into town. Regular gym sessions. Running becoming routine, not a novelty. Proper meals, consistently. A sharper look. Better clothes. A fresh haircut.
More time in the office. More presence. More energy.
In short, a version of life that feels switched on.
The version that’s been hovering in the background for a while now.
The Thing in the Way
And then there’s the part that complicates it.
Cannabis.

Not as a headline-grabbing scandal, but as a quiet, persistent drag. The thing that turns days into write-offs. That chips away at momentum. That makes everything just that bit harder than it needs to be.
It’s not dramatic. It’s familiar.
Which, in some ways, makes it harder to shift.
A Proper Test
This is where the promotion starts to matter.
Because if a moment like this doesn’t trigger change, what does?
There’s more money now. More structure. More reason to show up properly. Fewer excuses that actually hold up.
The argument from within the SwS camp is simple: the conditions have never been better.
So the outcome, this time, should be different.
Optimism — With a Catch
There’s confidence, certainly.
A sense that this time it sticks. That the new routine beds in. That the bike gets used, the gym becomes standard, the meals happen, the energy lifts.
That cannabis quietly drops out of the picture.
But there’s also realism.
Because this isn’t the first attempt. And habits like this don’t disappear just because circumstances improve.
They need replacing.
So, Will It Work?
That’s the open question.
The promotion provides the opening. The structure. The push.
But it doesn’t do the work on its own.
What follows over the next few weeks will be more telling than any announcement.
Because if the shift happens — properly, visibly — it won’t just be a career move.
It’ll be something bigger.
A reset.
And maybe, finally, an exit.

articles.title: SwS government moves to cut duplicate cycling costs after increased reliance on hire bikes
articles.standfirst: The Government of SwS is seeking to reduce duplicated transport spending after more than £75 was spent on Voi bikes despite an underutilised privately owned bicycle.

runs.text: The Government of SwS has announced a renewed focus on using its privately owned bicycle, citing concerns over duplicated spending after sustained use of city hire bikes despite already investing in a personal cycle.

In a press release published on 17 March, the Absurdist administration confirmed that cycling activity across SwS has been consistent, but largely delivered through the use of Voi-operated hire bicycles rather than the owned asset. Internal figures indicate that hire bikes have been used more than 20 times, with total expenditure exceeding £75.

This, the government suggests, represents an inefficient overlap in transport spending, given that the privately owned bicycle—purchased as part of a longer-term investment plan—has remained significantly underutilised.

The administration has linked this imbalance to previous storage arrangements. Until recently, the bicycle was housed in a Bikehangar on Gryffe Street, located approximately five minutes on foot from the SwS residence and positioned away from primary travel routes. While secure, the additional distance introduced what the government describes as a “persistent access barrier”, discouraging regular use.
By contrast, the Voi hire bikes—widely available across the city—offered immediate, on-route access, helping to establish a clear pattern of preference despite the higher cumulative cost.

To address this, the Government of SwS has relocated its bicycle storage to a Bikehangar on Battlefield Avenue. The new site sits directly along a principal movement corridor and within the same block as frequently accessed local services, significantly reducing the effort required to retrieve and use the bicycle.

The Absurdist administration assesses that this change removes a key friction point and will enable a shift away from paid hire usage towards the owned asset, improving both cost efficiency and transport autonomy.

As part of the policy reset, cycling will now be reinstated as a primary mode of transport for short and medium-distance journeys. The government has also introduced a structured set of recommended cycling routes connecting commonly visited destinations, including workplaces, leisure venues, and fitness facilities.

Initial routes prioritise segregated cycle infrastructure and shared-use paths, reflecting current confidence levels. However, the administration has indicated that more direct on-road routes may be incorporated over time as capability and familiarity increase.
The route mapping initiative is intended not only to guide immediate journeys but also to provide a framework for expanding cycling range across the city.

In parallel, additional equipment—including a pannier bag and helmet—has been acquired to support safer and more practical use. The total cost of these items was approximately £8 after applying reward credits from the original bicycle purchase.

The policy shift forms part of a wider effort under the Body piloti of the Government’s Four Pilotis framework, which governs physical health and mobility. While hire bikes are expected to remain a supplementary option, the administration has made clear that priority will now be given to maximising the value and utilisation of existing assets.
Cycling activity is expected to continue across both functional and recreational contexts, with further monitoring planned as part of the Spring/Summer 2026 governance programme.

articles.title: “I get FOMO about death”: Sam Smith on love, politics and learning to live with uncertainty
articles.standfirst: The 27-year-old BBC designer reflects on love in Glasgow’s Necropolis, political disillusionment, celebrity crushes from the 90s and why money, empathy and a sunny afternoon in the park still beat everything else.

runs.text: Sam Smith answers quickly, but not carelessly. The 27-year-old UX designer, who works on the BBC’s account and sign-in systems, has the air of someone who spends a lot of time thinking about how people interact with the world. His answers circle around empathy, freedom and the quiet details of everyday life.

Ask him when he was happiest and he doesn’t hesitate. “In the sun, in the summer, in Glasgow, in a park, with Adam.” The answer is simple and specific, the kind of scene that feels like it could repeat itself every year if you’re lucky.

Smith grew up in Glasgow and still speaks about the city with a mix of affection and political frustration. His biggest disappointment, he says bluntly, is “the Labour government of 2024 failing to do anything with its gigantic majority.” Politics matters to him, though he doesn’t treat it like a football team you support unconditionally. His views on Scottish independence have changed over time. In 2014 he worried that leaving the UK might mean leaving the EU and losing a sense of stability. Brexit and the chaos that followed, he says, changed that calculation entirely. “Now I think it’s time for us to get the hell out.”

For someone whose job involves designing systems used by millions of people, Smith is surprisingly candid about his own habits and flaws. The trait he most dislikes in himself is “waffling when I’m speaking”, though he admits that it sometimes comes from thinking through ideas in real time. What he struggles to tolerate in others is more fundamental: a lack of empathy, or people confidently presenting opinions about things they don’t understand.

His self-description is disarmingly direct: “Gay, twink, white.” Asked what he’d change about his appearance, he shrugs. “Maybe three extra inches in height.” Otherwise, he seems comfortable with who he is.

Love, for Smith, is about ease rather than intensity. It’s the feeling of being able to drop the filters we normally carry around with us. “Just being yourself around someone without fear of judgement,” he says. His most memorable kiss took place in Glasgow’s Necropolis cemetery with his boyfriend Adam, a moment he describes with a kind of quiet reverence. “It’s a very special place,” he says. “And it set me up for a lifetime of many more to come.”

Like many people in their twenties, Smith thinks about the future with a mix of ambition and mild existential dread. Growing older doesn’t scare him in the abstract; death does. “Eventually there comes a point where you die, and you don’t really have control over that,” he says. “I get FOMO.”
Money, he adds with a laugh, would be the most useful thing to have more of. “Money can be exchanged for goods and services,” he says, invoking a line from The Simpsons. “Including sex and fame.”

If life has taught him one principle worth holding onto, it’s the limits of perspective. “You can’t truly understand something from another person’s point of view,” he says. “The best thing you can do is assume good faith, try to embody empathy, and make the world a bit better with whatever you’re doing.”
As for what happens when we die, he pauses. The hopeful answer would be that something continues. The honest one, he says, is simpler. “Deep down, I think it probably just ends.”

Taken together, the BBC promotion bid and the University of London application form the core of the government’s current income-growth agenda. Both are high-pressure, high-stakes moves, and both will test SwS’s capacity to operate under sustained scrutiny.
There is confidence, but also realism. Success is far from guaranteed, and the coming months are expected to be demanding.
The outcome will shape not just earnings, but the future direction of the government itself.

articles.title: Government–commissioned report into Miniature Model Making
articles.standfirst: A government–commissioned report into the art of physical miniature model making

runs.text: 1. Purpose & Scope

Physical architectural models are three-dimensional representations of building designs, used by architects and designers to explore ideas, communicate concepts, and evaluate spatial relationships . Unlike digital models on a screen, physical models allow tactile interaction and true spatial understanding, letting both designers and laypeople grasp form and scale in a visceral way . Models are used throughout the design process – from rough concept massing studies to detailed presentation models – to test designs, inform decision-making, and present proposals . In professional practice and education alike, model making remains a valuable skill, complementing digital methods by providing a tangible perspective on the project .

Why modernist/brutalist buildings for beginners: Post-war modernist and brutalist architecture (such as Scottish new-town projects like Cumbernauld) features simple, massive forms and minimal ornamentation, making them ideal subjects for a first model. These designs emphasize massing, repetition, and structural clarity over intricate details. For example, brutalist structures often consist of bold geometric volumes in raw concrete, eliminating decorative details in favor of honest, straightforward forms . This means a beginner can capture the essence – the blocks, slabs and voids – without needing to reproduce fine ornament. The repetitive modular nature of housing blocks or civic buildings in this style provides practice in cutting and assembling multiple similar components, reinforcing skills through repetition. Moreover, modernist/brutalist models, even when simplified, have a strong visual presence that clearly conveys the architectural concept, which is encouraging for a newcomer.

Scope of this briefing: This document provides foundational guidance on starting from zero in physical model making. It covers the full process: from planning and design, choosing an appropriate scale, acquiring essential tools and materials, basic construction techniques, through to finishing and selecting a suitable first project. The focus is deliberately on beginner-level, hands-on advice – assuming no prior craft experience or equipment. What is not covered: advanced model-making techniques (e.g. laser cutting, 3D printing, complex detailing), professional presentation models, or broader architectural design theory beyond what’s needed to begin model building. The briefing also does not cover structural engineering or large-scale workshop fabrication – it is confined to table-top scale architectural models appropriate for a beginner. By adhering to the guidance here, a novice with strong design interest (especially in modernist/brutalist architecture) will be equipped to build their first simple building model and establish a foundation for more advanced projects.
2. Design & Planning (Digital → Physical)
Before cutting a single piece of card or foam, it’s wise to plan the model digitally or on paper. This section explains how to go from an initial architectural idea to a buildable model plan.

Using Shapr3D on iPad: A recommended approach for tech-savvy beginners is to use a 3D modeling app like Shapr3D on an iPad (with Apple Pencil) to sketch out the building form. Shapr3D provides an intuitive CAD interface where you can quickly create and adjust simple masses – perfect for modernist blocks and brutalist forms. Start by drawing the basic volumes of your building in the app: for example, a rectangular prism for a housing block, additional extruded forms for stair cores or balconies, etc. This digital massing model lets you explore proportions and geometry interactively. You can rotate and view it from all angles, ensuring the model will capture the key silhouettes and relationships. Use the app to establish an appropriate scale as well: model the building at real-world size (or import known dimensions), then decide on a scale (e.g. 1:100) and use the measurement tools to derive the model dimensions for each part. Shapr3D allows you to annotate or measure lengths, so you can note that, for instance, a 30m long facade will be 30 cm long in a 1:100 model. Some designers even export unrolled surfaces or drawings from Shapr3D as cutting templates – for example, one case study used a 1:10 scaled Shapr3D file to create an unrolled surface contour as a guide for cutting pieces out of card . You may similarly generate simple elevation outlines, print them to scale, and use them to trace shapes onto your material.

Level of precision vs. progress: At the beginning, perfect precision is not the goal – an approximation of form is usually sufficient for a concept model. A common pitfall is over-designing the model digitally. Remember that an architectural model is an abstraction; you do not need to model every window frame or door in CAD before building. Determine the overall size, proportions and key divisions (e.g. floor heights, major blocks) to a reasonable accuracy (within a few millimeters at model scale). That level of planning ensures pieces will fit, without getting bogged down in minor details. Know when to stop designing and start building: once the primary dimensions and volumes are decided and you’ve figured out how the pieces can be constructed, it’s time to move on. It’s often in the physical making that additional ideas or solutions will emerge, especially for beginners. Overly detailed digital plans can lead to frustration if they prove too difficult to realize in actual materials. So use digital tools to outline the form and test feasibility, but switch to physical building once you have a workable scheme. In short, design enough to be confident in scale and proportions, then let the real materials and process inform the rest.

Alternatives to digital planning: Digital modeling is helpful but not mandatory. Many beginners successfully plan with hand sketches and simple paper templates. You can draw scaled plans/elevations on graph paper or carton, then use those drawings as cutting guides. For instance, sketch the front view of your building at the target scale on paper; this becomes a template to cut out the facade in card. Similarly, drawing a floor plan outline on paper can guide your base and wall placements. Some modelers make “sketch models” from scrap materials early on – quick, rough constructions that aren’t glued permanently . Such sketch models (e.g. foam offcuts pinned together, or paper folded to shape) let you test the composition and massing in real 3D before committing to the final build. They are extremely useful to check if your design is too complex or if any part might be troublesome to construct. Because they’re temporary, you can adjust or discard them freely without feeling the pressure of perfection . In summary, whether using Shapr3D’s digital canvas or pencil-and-paper, aim to produce a clear but simple plan for the model’s form and measurements. Plan out how pieces will come together, then proceed to building – maintaining flexibility to adapt as you gain hands-on insight.
3. Scale Selection for Beginners

Choosing the right scale for your model is a crucial early decision. Scale affects not only the model’s size but also the level of detail you can (or should) include and the effort required . Scale in this context is the ratio of the model’s measurements to the real building. For example, at 1:100 scale, 1 centimeter on the model represents 1 meter on the real building. As a beginner, it’s important to select a scale that is manageable and suits your subject.

Recommended beginner scales: For a simple building such as a modest housing block, scales in the range of 1:100 to 1:200 are often ideal. At 1:100 (1cm = 1m), you can handle parts easily and represent major elements (walls, windows as openings, etc.) without the model becoming too large. A building of 30m length would be 30cm in the model – a convenient size for desk construction. 1:200 (0.5cm = 1m) is useful for larger structures or sites; it compresses space more, requiring less area, but also means small features like doorways might be only a few millimeters tall (often too fine for a beginner to cut accurately). Many architectural education projects use 1:100 or 1:200 for building models because they balance detail and simplicity. If your focus is a small house or a single room interior, 1:50 could be chosen (allowing more detail, like furniture blocks, since 1cm = 0.5m). Conversely, very large complexes or city massing might use 1:500 or 1:1000, but those scales significantly abstract away detail and can be challenging in a different way (tiny pieces, or very large context base). As a starting point, 1:100 is a good default for many modernist building models – it’s commonly used for building design models and offers a tangible level of detail without overwhelming size .

Trade-offs and scale discipline: Each scale comes with trade-offs between fidelity, size, and complexity. Larger scales (e.g. 1:50) produce bigger models where you can incorporate finer details (windows, texture, etc.), but the model will occupy more space and consume more material. Bigger models also take longer to build. Smaller scales (e.g. 1:200 or 1:500) yield compact models focusing on overall massing; they are faster in terms of fewer parts, but paradoxically can be harder for a beginner if too small, because tiny parts are fiddly to cut and assemble. In fact, “contrary to popular belief, smaller isn’t always faster” – choosing an overly small scale can lead to painstaking hours cutting miniature pieces that would have been unnecessary at a slightly larger scale . You should consider the amount of time and patience you have: it may be better to pick a larger scale and simplify the model’s scope, rather than a tiny scale that becomes frustrating . Once a scale is selected, discipline in its use is key. This means consistently converting real dimensions to model dimensions and maintaining those proportions throughout. Use a scale ruler (an architect’s triangular scale) set to your chosen ratio for quick measurements . For example, if using 1:100, a 10m wall should measure 10 cm on your model; check such conversions for all major parts. Plan for the thickness of materials at scale as well (e.g. a 5mm foamboard wall is 0.5m thick at 1:100 – appropriate for a concrete shear wall perhaps). Maintaining scale discipline ensures the model parts fit together correctly and that the finished piece accurately conveys the size relationships intended. Summary tip: Select the largest scale that still keeps your model within a convenient size, to maximize clarity and ease of building. And remember, the goal is to communicate the design’s essence – you can always indicate only the most important elements and omit the rest (more on that later) . By thoughtfully choosing and sticking to a scale, you set yourself up for a smoother build process and a legible result.
4. Tools: Acquisition & Setup

Building architectural models by hand requires a set of basic tools. This section outlines the absolute minimum toolkit needed, suggests useful upgrades, and covers safe use, maintenance, and budgeting – with a UK context for sourcing items.
Essential minimum tool list: Starting from nothing, you should acquire the following basic tools first:

Cutting implement: A sharp craft knife is the single most important tool. Common options are a utility knife with snap-off blades (e.g. Olfa 9mm), or a precision scalpel (such as a Swann-Morton handle with replaceable 10A blades) . Ensure you have a supply of spare blades. A sharp blade is crucial for clean cuts – and safer (dull blades slip and cause accidents) . A small pair of sharp scissors is also handy for thin card or paper details .

Cutting mat: A self-healing cutting mat (e.g. A3 or A2 size) provides a safe, durable surface for cutting . It protects your table and helps prolong blade life by offering a bit of “give”. Markings on the mat (grid or measurements) are useful for alignment.

Metal ruler (straightedge): A metal (steel or aluminum) ruler, 30 cm length to start (plus a shorter 15 cm for small pieces), is essential for guiding cuts and measuring . Plastic rulers will get sliced by your knife; a metal ruler with a non-slip backing or a cork strip is ideal. Ensure the edge is straight and true. Use the ruler for both measuring and as a straightedge to cut along.

Square / right-angle tool: A small try square or engineers’ square is very helpful for drawing and checking 90° angles . This ensures your model’s corners are straight and pieces align properly. Even a plastic drafting triangle can serve initially, though a solid metal square is more accurate.

Pencil and marker: A mechanical pencil, 0.5mm or thinner (0.3mm HB or H leads), is recommended for marking cut lines precisely without tearing the material . Also have a softer pencil or fine-tip marker to label pieces lightly on non-visible sides if needed. An eraser for removing guidelines is useful.

Adhesives: At minimum, get PVA white glue (wood glue or school glue) for general assembly of card, wood, foam – it’s strong and dries clear (albeit slowly) . Also consider a pack of cyanoacrylate (super glue) for instant bonding of small pieces or dissimilar materials . Masking tape (low-tack painter’s tape) is very useful to hold pieces together temporarily while glue sets, and for marking guidelines.

Support tools: A few pins or clips to hold parts (you can use common push pins, or binder clips for clamping edges) help during gluing . Gather some sandpaper (medium ~120 grit and fine ~300 grit) to smooth rough edges and gently bevel or clean cuts . Also have a rag or paper towels for wiping excess glue, and a small sanding block (could just be a flat wood offcut wrapped in sandpaper) for keeping edges straight while sanding.

With the above, you can accomplish the basic tasks of cutting, measuring, and gluing accurately. This toolkit is generally affordable. For example, in the UK a beginner could acquire a decent knife, mat, ruler, glue, and some sundries for on the order of £30–£50 total (available from art and stationery shops or online).
Recommended beginner upgrades (nice-to-have):

Additional cutting tools: Extra knife types (e.g. a heavier-duty Stanley knife for thick foam, a smaller hobby knife for fine cuts) can be useful. A circle cutter or compass cutter helps in cutting neat circles or arcs in card.
Set of files or micro-sanders: For fine tuning edges, small needle files or an emery board can refine windows or door openings after cutting.

Clamps and weights: A set of small clamps or even reusable heavy objects (metal blocks, small hand vise, or bulldog clips) will secure pieces while glue dries and ensure right angles . Having a couple of metal 90° angle blocks or Lego® bricks can serve as jigs to keep walls perpendicular during assembly.

Tweezers or pliers: Fine-tipped tweezers help in placing small components or pulling glue strings. Small pliers or wire cutters are needed if you work with any wire or pins (for instance, clipping pins used as alignment dowels).

Expanded measuring tools: A triangular scale ruler with multiple scales (1:50, 1:100, 1:200, etc.) simplifies measuring in scale . Also, digital calipers are an optional precision tool if you want to directly measure small lengths accurately (useful but not essential early on).

Cutting aids: A metal safety ruler with a finger guard can protect your hand during cutting. A straightedge with cork back helps keep it from slipping. Also, consider a matte cutter or miniature mitre box if you plan to cut a lot of 90° miters (e.g. in wood strips for frames).

Specialty tools (later on): As you progress, you might invest in tools like a hot wire cutter (for shaping foam with smooth curves), a small tabletop saw (for wood strips), or even time-saving devices like laser-cutting services (some universities or makerspaces offer laser cutting for model parts). These are not needed for initial projects, but you should know they exist for future. For example, laser cutting can precisely cut acrylic, wood, or card for complex models – but it requires learning CAD drafting for cutting and isn’t typically a beginner’s first step .
Tool safety and maintenance: Safety is paramount when using cutting tools and adhesives:

Cutting safety: Always use a sharp blade and proper technique. Never force a dull blade; replace or sharpen it frequently – “accidents often happen with blunt blades because unnecessary pressure is put on the blade, making it easier to slip” . Cut away from your body and hands. Use a ruler as a guide and keep fingers clear of the blade path (some model-makers even wear a cut-resistant glove on the hand holding the ruler for protection). Make multiple light passes with the knife rather than one heavy cut ; this gives better control and avoids snapping blades. Always retract or cover blades when not in use.

Glue and fumes: Work in a well-ventilated area, especially if using solvent-based glues or spray adhesives. Solvent cements (for plastic) and aerosol sprays should be used with windows open or under an extractor, and keep them away from open flames. Super glue can bond skin instantly – wear nitrile gloves or use tweezers for tiny parts, and have acetone handy to debond if needed. Hot glue guns can cause burns; be cautious and use the low-temperature setting if available.

Workspace setup: Ensure you have good lighting over your work area – proper lighting prevents eye strain and cutting errors . Clear a sufficient, stable workspace so you can lay out parts without clutter. Keep a bin for offcuts nearby to immediately dispose of scraps and maintain order . An organized area will prevent accidents (like knocking over a knife or losing sharp blades in a mess).

Maintenance: Store tools dry and clean. Wipe excess glue off applicators and blades before it hardens. For knives, change blades often and dispose of used blades in a sharps container (an old screw-top jar works). Cutting mats last a long time but avoid excessive force that could gouge them; you can rotate the mat periodically so you’re not always cutting in the same groove. If using any power tools (drills, etc.), follow the manufacturer’s safety instructions and wear safety glasses.

Budgeting and sourcing (UK): Getting started need not be expensive. Basic toolkits are available from general craft retailers like Hobbycraft or online marketplaces (Amazon, eBay). Look also at art supply stores such as Cass Art (which carries model-making materials and tools) . For specialty items, the UK has dedicated model-making suppliers – for example, 4D Modelshop in London offers a vast range of raw materials and tools for models (styrene plastic sheets, foam, card, blades, etc.), available via mail order. Even general hardware stores (B&Q, Screwfix) can supply items like knives, blades, and insulation foam. When budgeting, prioritize the essentials mentioned; you can always add tools as needed per project. For instance, buy a quality knife and mat now, and postpone purchasing a hot wire cutter or fancy foam cutter until you actually require it. UK-specific tips: Surgical scalpels (Swann-Morton) and spare blades are inexpensive and high-quality, widely available online. PVA glue (often called wood glue or white glue) comes from brands like Evo-Stik, Gorilla or UniBond, all fine for paper/wood. For foam-safe adhesive, look for solvent-free formulas (standard PVA is safe on foam; solvent glues are not). Many art shops stock A1 or A2 foamboard sheets and mount board, and balsa wood strips, often in their technical drawing or architecture section. In summary, start with a core set of tools that fit your budget and add to your toolbox as your projects grow in complexity. Proper tools are an investment – “invest in high-quality tools because they last longer and give better results” – but even on a tight budget, you can obtain the necessary items to begin model making safely and effectively.
5. Materials: Selection & Use

Choosing the right materials is as important as having the right tools. Different materials have different properties that affect ease of use, appearance, and durability of your model . As a beginner focusing on modernist/brutalist buildings, you will work mostly with a few core, versatile materials. Below we introduce the main materials recommended for starter architectural models – foam board, XPS foam, mountboard (card), plasticard, and balsa wood – explaining when and why to use each, their behavior and handling, and tips on storage and longevity.

Foam Board (Foamcore): Description: Foam board consists of a sheet of polystyrene (foam) sandwiched between two thin paper/card faces. It usually comes in white (also black or other colors) and in various thicknesses (commonly 3mm, 5mm) . Why use: Foam board is lightweight, strong for its weight, and easy to cut, making it ideal for quick massing of building forms . It produces a clean, neutral look – all surfaces smooth and flat – great for modernist forms (often used for all-white concept models) . Corners and junctions can be very neat because the foam core allows precise slicing and joins at 90° . Behavior & handling: Use a sharp knife and multiple light cuts to slice foam board without tearing the paper face . A metal straightedge guide is essential for straight cuts. You can also score one face (cut partially through) and then bend the board to form sharp-edged folds for certain shapes . When gluing, PVA white glue works well – apply thinly to avoid saturating the paper. Hot glue can also be used for instant bonds (the foam core accepts hot glue, but work quickly as it sets fast) . Solvent-based glues or paints should be avoided on foam board because they can melt the foam interior . Limitations: Foam board’s paper surfaces can warp if overly wetted by glue or paint – use glue sparingly and let it dry flat. The foam core is somewhat fragile: edges can dent, and exposed foam at cut edges is soft (corner joints might need reinforcement if load-bearing pieces). It’s not ideal for fine detail or very thin slivers (they will crush). Storage & longevity: Store foam boards flat to prevent bending, and in a dry environment (moisture can cause the paper to bow or delaminate). If kept indoors away from UV light and moisture, foam board models last many years, but note that the foam can yellow slightly over time and the paper may attract dust or discolor. For a durable presentation model, some prefer more robust materials, but for concept and practice models foam board is excellent .

XPS Foam (Insulation Foam): Description: Extruded polystyrene (XPS) foam is a dense foam often sold in insulation boards (commonly blue, pink, gray, or green sheets). Unlike foamcore, it is solid foam without paper facings. It’s sometimes called “styrofoam” in the US (though technically different) or informally “blue foam” after a popular type . Why use: XPS foam is extremely useful for massing studies and topography because it’s very quick to cut and shape . It comes in various thicknesses (5mm up to several centimeters), allowing easy creation of blocks for buildings or layered contours for landscapes . Architects BIG and OMA are known to use foam extensively in conceptual models . It’s lightweight and can be stacked or carved to produce complex forms rapidly. For brutalist subjects, foam can represent solid concrete volumes nicely (painted or unpainted). Behavior & handling: XPS foam cuts with a sharp blade (utility knife) – cut in shallow passes to avoid ragged edges. It also sands well: you can use sandpaper to refine shapes or even create slopes. A hot wire cutter is an optional tool that slices foam smoothly with a heated wire; if you have access to one, it allows very clean cuts and curved slicing, but always use it in ventilated space (melting foam releases fumes) . Glues: Use PVA or wood glue for most XPS foam joins; it adheres well (though drying takes a bit of time). Hot glue can also bond foam quickly, but be cautious – too hot and it can melt a bit of foam, and once stuck it’s hard to reposition. Avoid solvent-based adhesives (like model airplane glue or spray mount with solvents), as they will melt the foam . If you need to attach foam to foam strongly, toothpicks or cocktail sticks can serve as internal pins along with glue. Limitations: XPS foam is fragile under impact – edges and corners dent easily if pressed. Its surface is slightly rough (especially some types that are “bubbly” inside), so it may not give a refined finish for close-up viewing. It’s best for underlayers or rough massing rather than small detail parts. Also, painting requires care: spray paint will dissolve foam unless you first prime it (e.g. with an acrylic gesso or a coat of PVA). Acrylic model paints can be applied by brush as they are water-based. For a “concrete” finish, you might coat foam with a thin layer of filler or plaster, or use a texture paint (more on finishes later). Storage: Keep XPS foam sheets flat, not leaning (to avoid warping). Store in a bag or covered, as the static can attract dirt to the surface. It doesn’t mind humidity in terms of shape, but avoid high heat which could deform it. Longevity: Foam massing models are usually for early design phases – the material can last, but pieces might chip if handled frequently. For a final model, foam might be used internally and clad or painted for protection. In general, insulation foam is a forgiving, inexpensive material that invites quick experimentation – perfect for beginners to cut their teeth (sometimes literally – with a blade!) on basic forms .

Mountboard / Cardboard: Description: Mount board (mounting board) is a thick cardboard typically used for mounting photographs or art. It often has a smooth colored face (white/black/grey) and a cardboard core, around 1.5mm thick (there are also thinner presentation boards and thicker chipboards). More generally, cardstock and cardboard of various types fall in this category of paper-based sheet materials. Why use: Card is cheap, readily available, and versatile . It’s great for planar elements: walls, bases, or simple facade panels. Mountboard in particular is stiff and can hold its shape well for medium-sized models . It can represent neutral surfaces or be painted. Because it’s paper-based, it’s easy to cut (though thicker boards need more effort) and is a classic material for architectural models for both conceptual and semi-detailed models . For a brutalist motif, a grey card can directly suggest concrete color, or layers of card can simulate stratified ground or building levels . Behavior & handling: Use a sharp scalpel or utility knife; cut in multiple passes to avoid crushing the edges . When cutting thick mountboard, try to keep the blade perpendicular to avoid angled edges. Blades will dull quickly on dense card – replace or sharpen frequently . Card edges can be sanded lightly with fine sandpaper to smooth or bevel them. Gluing: PVA works well (especially PVA wood glue which grabs a bit faster and stronger on paper) . Apply glue sparingly and spread thinly – card absorbs moisture and too much glue can warp it. A thicker “tacky glue” (a common craft glue) is often preferred for card because it has less water content and sets faster . Another method is using double-sided tape or spray adhesive for large flat pieces – these give instant bonds and no warping, though placement must be precise (they’re hard to reposition) . Limitations: Cardboard is not as dimensionally stable as plastic or wood; long thin strips may bend. It’s best for relatively short spans or where both edges will be glued to something. Exposed edges of multi-ply card show the layers – sometimes that’s acceptable, sometimes not (you can cover edges with paper or filler if needed). Also, cutting small openings (like tiny windows) in thick card can be tricky to do cleanly. For very fine work, thinner card (or switch to plastic) might be easier. Handling tips: When marking on dark card, use a white pencil or chalk pencil; for light card, a hard pencil or even scoring lightly can mark cut lines. Scoring and bending: You can score halfway through and fold card to make corners (similar to foam board technique), useful for making a crisp corner without a separate joint. Storage: Keep card sheets flat and dry. If they do warp, you can sometimes flatten them under heavy books or press gently opposite to the bend. Avoid humidity and direct sunlight (sun can cause fading of colored card). Longevity: Good quality mountboard is often acid-free and can last decades if kept dry. However, if exposed to moisture or fluctuating humidity, card models can distort. Also, card is a paper product – it can attract insects or mold in poor conditions. For a lasting model, you might seal or paint the card surfaces to protect them. In summary, cardboard is a fundamental material for model-making due to its affordability and versatility – from baseplates to building shells, it will likely feature in your first project .

Plasticard (Styrene Plastic Sheets): Description: “Plasticard” usually refers to sheets of polystyrene or ABS plastic sold for hobby modeling. These are smooth, white (or colored) plastic sheets in thicknesses from ~0.25mm up to a few millimeters. Polystyrene sheet (also called styrene sheet) is common for scratch-building models, as it’s easy to cut and glue with solvent. Why use: Plastic sheet can produce very crisp, clean models with precise detail. It is dimensionally stable (doesn’t warp with normal glue or paint if used properly) and allows finer detail than card – e.g. scoring panel lines to represent facade joints, cutting very thin strips for railings, etc. For a brutalist model, plastic sheet could be useful if you want to achieve sharp-edged facades or repeatable modules (since plastic can be laser-cut or scored with high precision). It also takes paint well, so you can get a uniform concrete-like finish. Behavior & handling: Thin styrene sheets can be cut by scoring with a knife and snapping. For example, use a knife to draw a deep line (without cutting through entirely), then bend the sheet which will snap cleanly along the score . For thicker plastic (>1mm), you may need to saw gently with a fine-tooth model saw or make many passes with a knife. Filing and sanding plastic is very effective – edges can be smoothed and shaped with sandpaper (plastics file easily to refine shapes). One can also heat-bend plastic for curves, but that’s advanced. Gluing: The preferred glue is solvent cement (plastic weld glue) which actually melts and fuses the plastic at the joint, creating a very strong bond and seamless look . Applied with a brush, the solvent glue (like Plastic Weld, MEK, or Tamiya Extra Thin cement) will join styrene pieces in seconds to minutes. This is excellent for assembling plastic parts but use sparingly and in ventilated conditions (the fumes are strong). Alternatively, cyanoacrylate (super glue) works on styrene and ABS as well, giving instant bonds without melting – good for attaching plastic to other materials (like plastic to wood, or to foam, though be careful as super glue can melt some foams). Hot glue is not recommended for plastic sheet – it doesn’t adhere well and the thickness of hot glue can misalign parts. Limitations: Cutting plastic cleanly requires practice; if you only have a knife, very intricate cuts can be tedious (plastics aren’t as forgiving as card for cutting tight corners).
