articles.title: Three days until DIBI
articles.standfirst: DIBI returns to Edinburgh in three days for two packed days of product, design and technology talks at Dynamic Earth.

runs.text: DIBI conference branding at an earlier event. Image: HeadBox / The Biscuit Room.
Three days until DIBI
DIBI is back in Edinburgh this week, with the two-day digital product and technology conference due to open at Dynamic Earth on Wednesday 30 September.

The event, which runs into Thursday 1 October, bills itself around “actionable insights for product people” and brings design, development and product thinking together rather than treating them as separate disciplines. For a UX practice increasingly concerned with experimentation, evidence and how design operates inside wider product systems, that makes this year’s programme particularly well timed.

DIBI says its speakers are intended to inform, challenge and inspire across commercial, creative and technical domains. Product designer Joel Miller of Figma is among the names currently promoted by organisers, while Herb Kim is returning as host. Alongside the talks, the conference includes practical workshops and networking across the two days.

The timing lands during a busy stretch of design work. The BBC calendar shows Experiment Enablement UX stand-ups continuing this week, alongside a Data UX check-in on Tuesday. A separate session on opportunities for experimentation in product engineering teams has been cancelled pending clearer H2 planning outcomes, a small but telling reminder that the organisational conditions around experimentation remain in motion.

That context matters. Recent experimentation work has repeatedly surfaced questions about ownership, measurement confidence, governance and the point at which specialist input enters the process. DIBI’s broad product-and-tech framing offers a useful chance to look beyond individual UX methods and towards how design decisions survive contact with engineering, commercial constraints and organisational reality.

There is also a strong practical streak to the event. Organisers promise workshops built around tools, techniques and ideas that attendees can apply directly in their roles. That emphasis should help separate the conference from the familiar circuit of inspirational design talks that sound good on stage but struggle to make it into Monday morning’s work.
Dynamic Earth will host the conference again, placing the event beside Holyrood in central Edinburgh. Conference passes are currently advertised at £255 excluding VAT.

With three days to go, the interesting question is less whether DIBI can produce another round of polished product talks and more whether its mix of design, development and business thinking can offer anything genuinely useful for the messier work now happening around experimentation.
For
SWS.GOV
, that is the bit worth watching.

articles.title: SWS.GOV gets a proper backlog
articles.standfirst: A new Notion board brings SWS.GOV work into one backlog, with dedicated views across the site and a simple to-do, doing and done workflow.

runs.text: Project board logo. Source: Wikimedia Commons.
SWS.GOV
gets a proper backlog
SWS.GOV
has moved its redesign work into a single project board, giving Project Indigo a clearer route from idea to done.

The new setup uses a straightforward Kanban workflow: to do, doing and done. It is deliberately simple, but the board is split into dedicated views for the main parts of the site, including the homepage, recipes, goals, planner, archive, iFit, bookshelf, news, reader and search, alongside an all-projects view.
That matters because
SWS.GOV

is no longer one redesign job. Project Indigo has grown into a rolling rebuild touching the site’s visual language, navigation and a string of individual services. The homepage is becoming a personalised dashboard, search is expanding beyond the archive, News has become an active publishing stream, and older areas such as Recipes and Archive are being reworked rather than simply reskinned.

Until now, much of that work has lived across conversations, prototypes, code and individual decisions. The new project board gives those moving parts a common operational layer. Each ticket can carry basic information and its own tasks, while filtered views mean a homepage job can sit in the same underlying system as a Planner or Bookshelf job without turning the board into a wall of noise.

The change is modest compared with the visible parts of Indigo, but it tackles a familiar product-design problem: once a project becomes broad enough, the work around the work starts to matter. A redesign can look coherent in Figma while the delivery backlog quietly fragments across notes and memory.
For
SWS.GOV

, the immediate consequence is less glamorous but more useful. There is now one place to see what is waiting, what is active and what has actually shipped, without losing the ability to focus on one service at a time.

The board also arrives at a useful point in Indigo’s rollout. The redesign is intended to continue progressively through the end of 2026, which means old and new parts of the site will coexist for a while. That makes prioritisation more important: unfinished work is no longer just a list of design ideas, but a live queue against a site already changing underneath it.

The test now is whether the board stays current. A Kanban system only earns its keep when tickets move with the work. If that happens, Project Indigo has gained something it badly needed: not another feature, but a proper backlog.

articles.title: A small offer becomes a poster
articles.standfirst: A fleeting offer of help on Battlefield Road has become the latest raw material for an increasingly everyday strand of poster-making.

runs.text: Battlefield Road in Glasgow’s Southside. Image: Scotland’s Property Guide.
A small offer becomes a poster
A two-second exchange on Battlefield Road has ended up doing something rather bigger than expected: becoming the subject of a new poster experiment.

The moment itself was almost aggressively ordinary. Walking along the Glasgow Southside street, Sam Smith spotted a man trying to get through a doorway while pushing a pram. With the door proving awkward, Smith offered a hand and moved to hold it open.
“Do you need a hand, mate?” was the offer. The man replied that he was all right, and the pair carried on with their day.

That could easily have been the end of it. Instead, the tiny encounter was later turned into a visual study, using the real streetscape as the setting and stripping the incident back to its basic ingredients: a pavement, a doorway, two strangers and an offer that was not actually needed.

The first version treated the scene fairly literally before the direction shifted towards something more avant-garde. Excess text was removed and the real location became more important, leaving the image to carry most of the story rather than explaining the event in words.

It is a small development, but it fits a wider pattern in recent creative work. Posters have increasingly become less about waiting for a suitably grand subject and more about treating everyday material as something worth designing around. That can mean a piece of music, a personal joke, a local place or, in this case, a social interaction lasting only seconds.

The result also captures something recognisable about city life. Offers of help are made, declined and forgotten constantly. There was no rescue, no dramatic intervention and no reason to inflate the exchange into one. The man with the pram said he was fine. Smith accepted that. Everyone moved on.

That lack of drama is precisely what made the incident useful as visual material. Rather than presenting the moment as an act of heroism, the poster can focus on the awkward choreography of two people briefly negotiating the same doorway and then separating again.

The setting matters too. Battlefield Road is not an abstract backdrop but part of the everyday geography of home: sandstone tenements, shopfronts, traffic and the repeated routes of ordinary Southside life. Using it directly pushes the work closer to a kind of personal visual record rather than a generic design exercise.
The poster remains an experiment rather than a major project. But the underlying idea is potentially more durable: make things from what is already happening, instead of waiting for a perfect brief.
On Wednesday, that meant a man, a pram and a door. By Thursday, it had become another entry in a growing visual archive of everyday life.

articles.title: Comedy night at the King’s
articles.standfirst: A planned Glasgow comedy night put Vittorio Angelone on the King’s Theatre stage as his latest UK tour reached the city.

runs.text: Vittorio Angelone on his 2026 tour. Image: Vittorio Angelone official website / Just the Tonic Comedy Club.
Comedy night at the King’s
Vittorio Angelone brought his latest stand-up show to Glasgow on Thursday, taking over the King’s Theatre for a 7.30pm date on his 2026 UK tour.

The Northern Irish comic arrived in the city on 24 September as part of a run that continues to Leeds on 28 September. The Glasgow performance was listed by both the venue and British Comedy Guide, making the King’s one of the larger traditional theatres on a tour built around Angelone’s fast-growing live audience.

Angelone’s route into comedy was not especially conventional. His official biography says he grew up in Belfast before moving to London to train as a classical musician, later switching to stand-up. He has since completed sell-out tours and appeared at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

His first Edinburgh run also brought a nomination for Best Newcomer at the Edinburgh Comedy Awards in 2022. Since then, online clips, sketches and podcast appearances have helped turn him into a recognisable name well beyond the club circuit.

The current show, You Can’t Say Nothing Anymore, continues a style that plays with uncomfortable subjects and the tension around what can and cannot be joked about. Angelone has previously said that he works to keep the jokes from becoming nasty or mean, while still taking an audience towards ideas they may find uncomfortable.

That combination has made the live show a more interesting prospect than a straightforward night of safe observational comedy. It also fits a wider strand of contemporary stand-up in which podcasts and short online clips sit alongside the traditional touring circuit, allowing performers to build a sizeable audience before television becomes the main route to recognition.

The King’s Theatre date placed that newer comedy career inside one of Glasgow’s most traditional entertainment venues. The theatre has long hosted touring drama, musicals, comedy and pantomime, giving the night a deliberately old-school setting for a performer whose audience has been built in a very modern way.
For
SWS.GOV

, the Glasgow stop lands as a cultural break in a busy late-September stretch dominated by design work, experimentation and personal projects. It also comes just days before the DIBI design conference begins in Edinburgh, shifting the diary from live comedy back towards product, technology and design.
One night, one microphone and a packed theatre is a fairly simple proposition. In a week full of systems, prototypes and planning, that simplicity is part of the point.

articles.title: The casino floor looks familiar
articles.standfirst: A casino-floor thought experiment has turned into a sharper look at the design mechanics shared by slot machines and attention-hungry digital products.

runs.text: Slot machines at the Model T Casino in Winnemucca, Nevada. Image: Mx. Granger / Wikimedia Commons, CC0.
The casino floor looks familiar
A grim casino-floor thought experiment has opened up a much bigger design question: how different is a slot machine, really, from the digital products fighting to keep people tapping and scrolling?

The comparison came after a discussion about the extreme pull of slot machines, from people sitting at machines for hours to the strange tunnel vision that can make everything else in the room feel irrelevant. The uncomfortable follow-up was closer to home. Endless social feeds can produce a milder version of the same basic feeling: one more pull, one more refresh, one more clip.

That does not make Instagram a casino, and scrolling is not financially equivalent to gambling. But the overlap in interaction design is hard to miss. Both can use rapid feedback, uncertain rewards and frictionless repetition to turn a tiny action into a loop.

The evidence around gambling machines is particularly stark. Research has linked the rapid, continuous nature of electronic gaming machines with sustained play, while studies of near-misses have found that apparently almost-winning can increase arousal and distort a player's sense of control. The UK's Gambling Commission has explicitly treated product design as a safety issue rather than a cosmetic one.

Its rules for online slots now ban autoplay, features that speed up play, spins faster than 2.5 seconds and celebratory sounds or imagery when a player has actually lost money overall on the spin. The regulator says the aim is to reduce intensity and stop products exploiting or encouraging problem gambling behaviour. A later assessment found evidence that the 2021 changes reduced play intensity without producing harmful unintended consequences.
For
SWS.GOV
, the interesting bit is the UX lesson.

Designers usually talk about reducing friction as though it is automatically good. Make the next action obvious. Remove unnecessary steps. Keep momentum. Reward engagement. In most services that can be sensible. But a casino floor is a fairly brutal demonstration of what happens when an experience becomes exceptionally good at keeping somebody inside a loop whose interests are not necessarily aligned with theirs.
The same question applies, with very different stakes, to feeds, short-form video, notifications and other attention products. A successful interaction metric can still describe a poor human outcome.

That makes the casino comparison less a claim that all persuasive design is addictive and more a useful stress test. If an interface is optimised to make stopping harder, what exactly is being improved?
The answer matters well beyond gambling. The strongest design may sometimes be the design that gives people a clean way out.

articles.title: A free hour lands on Friday
articles.standfirst: BBC Product Group staff have been given a free hour next Friday to switch off and spend time on something for themselves.

runs.text: BBC Scotland at Pacific Quay in Glasgow. Image: Batchelor/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
A free hour lands on Friday
BBC staff in the Product Group are being handed an extra hour next Friday with one instruction: use it for yourself.

A Free Hour has appeared in the BBC calendar for 14:00 to 15:00 on Friday 2 October, extending an initiative already being used by some teams across the wider Product Group. The calendar note says colleagues should switch off and spend the time doing something just for them.

The suggestions are deliberately ordinary. A walk, meeting a friend or doing some gardening are all offered as examples. There is no workshop, no output and no request to turn the hour into another piece of professional development.
For a working week built around stand-ups, reviews, catch-ups and delivery, that absence of an agenda is the point.

The hour arrives at the end of a busy stretch in the work diary. The coming week includes regular team check-ins, UX stand-ups, a sprint review and a session on end-to-end work, alongside the DIBI Conference in Edinburgh on 30 September and 1 October.
That makes the timing notable. Instead of filling another available slot, the invitation deliberately protects one.

The free hour lands on Friday, which is separately marked as a non-working day in the BBC calendar. The practical effect may therefore vary depending on individual working patterns, but the Product Group invitation itself is explicit: the time is intended for switching off rather than squeezing in another task.

The move fits a broader BBC approach that has long linked working practices with wellbeing. Public BBC flexible-working policy describes work-life balance as relevant to motivation, performance, productivity and stress. The organisation's health and attendance policy also says managers have a role in supporting the health and wellbeing of their teams.

This particular initiative is much smaller and more immediate than a formal policy change. It is an hour in the diary, not a new employment entitlement, and the calendar wording makes no wider promise about how often it will happen.

But its simplicity is arguably what makes it noticeable. Modern knowledge work has a habit of colonising spare gaps with messages, admin and quick meetings. Blocking an hour and explicitly telling people not to optimise it into more work cuts against that instinct.

There is also something refreshingly specific about the examples. Nobody is being asked to meditate, complete a wellbeing module or demonstrate that the hour was productive. Walking, seeing a friend or gardening are enough.
For teams working largely through digital calendars and collaboration tools, the intervention is almost comically low-tech: put an hour in the diary and give it back.
No grand programme. No deliverable. Just 60 minutes back.

articles.title: Paris palace faces the value test
articles.standfirst: A Paris luxury stay is under consideration as the Four Seasons George V is weighed against the premium attached to one of the city’s grandest hotels.

runs.text: Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris. Photo: Alan Light/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Paris palace faces the value test
One of Paris’s grandest hotels has landed on the travel shortlist, but the question is not whether it is luxurious. It is whether that luxury is actually worth paying for.

The Four Seasons Hotel George V, just off the Champs-Élysées in the capital’s Golden Triangle, is being weighed as a possible stay. It is an Art Deco landmark dating from 1928, with 243 rooms and suites, a spa and pool, and three restaurants carrying six Michelin stars between them in the 2026 guide.

That makes the George V an unusually complete luxury proposition. Le Cinq has now held three Michelin stars for ten consecutive years under chef Christian Le Squer, while L’Orangerie retains two and Le George one. The hotel’s accommodation ranges from 37–40 sq m Superior Rooms to vast signature suites, with some rooms and suites offering terraces, balconies or Eiffel Tower views.
But
SWS.GOV

’s interest is less about ticking off luxury credentials than testing the value equation. A spectacular lobby, elaborate flowers and attentive service can make a hotel feel like part of the trip rather than somewhere to sleep. The catch is that this only works if enough time is actually spent there to enjoy it.

For a Paris visit built around long days in the city, restaurants, museums and wandering neighbourhoods, a palace hotel can become an extremely expensive base for showering and sleeping. The George V makes a stronger case when the hotel itself is deliberately treated as an experience: breakfast in, time at the pool or spa, a drink in La Galerie, and enough breathing room to appreciate the service and surroundings.

There is also a design argument. The hotel sits firmly in the traditional grand-Paris category rather than the stripped-back Scandinavian look often favoured elsewhere. Its interiors combine historic Art Deco character, classical French furniture and contemporary pieces. That makes it a fairly maximalist choice, but also a chance to experience a kind of hospitality design that would be difficult to reproduce at a normal city hotel.
No booking decision has been made. For now, the George V remains in the category of tempting extravagance rather than obvious value.

The verdict is therefore awkwardly simple: the hotel appears capable of justifying its reputation, but not automatically its price. If the stay becomes part of the holiday, the maths gets easier. If Paris itself is the whole point, the money may be better kept for Paris.

articles.title: Artwork gets the green light
articles.standfirst: A finished album-art experiment has cleared its final design pass and is ready to carry Sam Smith’s name in public.

runs.text: A coloured vinyl record on an Audio-Technica turntable. Picture: M. Johnson/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Artwork gets the green light

A new piece of album artwork is ready to leave the drafts folder after a final design pass on Wednesday, turning a quick visual experiment into something Sam Smith is prepared to put his name on and publish.

The work was developed and refined during a wider burst of poster-making and graphic experimentation. The finished version was reviewed again on 23 September, with attention shifting from whether the concept worked at all to the smaller details that separate a promising draft from a piece that feels finished: hierarchy, spacing, balance and the treatment of individual elements.

That matters because the project sits inside a broader push to make personal design work more visible rather than leaving it as private practice. Recent plans include keeping poster-making running in the background while building a simple place to sell selected work through a dropship model. The album artwork is not itself a confirmed commercial release, but it is another piece of evidence that the creative pipeline is becoming more regular and more public-facing.

The timing is useful. A separate planning exercise this week pulled five active strands into one Notion-based system, including the poster shop, personal finances, Blender experiments, England Weekend Television and outreach connected to that project. The aim is less about adding another productivity layer and more about stopping good ideas from competing for the same bit of mental space.

Wednesday’s artwork review also showed a shift in the standard being applied. The question was no longer simply whether the image looked good enough. It became whether individual components could still be improved before the name went on it. That is a more demanding test, and a healthier one for work intended to sit alongside professional design output.

There is no announced release date, client or record attached to the artwork, and it should not be mistaken for a commissioned sleeve. For now it remains a self-directed design piece. But it has crossed a small threshold: from experiment to finished work worth sharing. With a poster storefront also on the agenda, that distinction could become increasingly important as more of the personal archive moves into public view.

articles.title: A wee exhibition became something bigger
articles.standfirst: A trip to Get Glasgow Moving’s tenth-anniversary exhibition turned into a small but useful test of what happens when anxiety stops getting the final say.

runs.text: A wee exhibition became something bigger
An illustrated view of a transport exhibition, created for
SWS.GOV
I nearly didn’t go.

Get Glasgow Moving’s tenth-anniversary exhibition at the New Glasgow Society was exactly the sort of thing I’d normally be interested in: Glasgow, public transport, civic campaigning and people trying to make the city work better. The campaign itself was founded in 2016, and the exhibition looks back over its first decade.
The problem was the bit between being interested in it and actually walking through the door.

I was going on my own. I didn’t know exactly what the room would be like, who would be there or whether I’d end up awkwardly having to speak to people. None of that was especially dramatic, but it was enough for my brain to start producing reasons not to bother.
I went anyway.
Once I was inside, the whole thing became considerably less intimidating. I looked around the exhibition, spoke briefly to the people there and bought an orange Get Glasgow Moving T-shirt.
That should probably be the end of the story. Person goes to exhibition. Person enjoys exhibition. Person buys T-shirt.
But the interesting bit was how badly the anxiety beforehand predicted the actual experience.
Getting through the door

The New Glasgow Society describes itself as a civic society focused on Glasgow’s beauty, history and character, using campaigning, discussion, projects, talks and exhibitions. Get Glasgow Moving, meanwhile, is a grassroots campaign for a more integrated, accessible and publicly accountable public transport network across the region.
In other words, this was not a random social obligation. It sat almost absurdly neatly at the intersection of things I care about.
That makes the instinct to avoid it more interesting.

I’ve started thinking about the difference between discomfort that is genuinely telling you something useful and discomfort that is simply the price of doing something unfamiliar. I’m very good at building systems that make life comfortable. Usually that is sensible. But comfort can quietly become a decision-making framework of its own.
The exhibition was a tiny example of what happens when it isn’t.
I didn’t suddenly become an extrovert. I didn’t spend the afternoon networking with everyone in the room. Nothing transformative happened in the conventional sense.
I just went in.
From watching to joining in
The more important thought came while I was there.

I’ve followed organisations like Get Glasgow Moving for years. I’m interested in how Glasgow works, how it moves and how it could be better. But there is an easy habit of treating the people who actually organise things, campaign, speak publicly and participate in civic life as a separate category of person.
Standing in the exhibition, that distinction felt a bit daft.
There is no fundamental reason I couldn’t eventually be one of the people contributing to something like this rather than simply following it from the outside.
The difficult part is making sure this does not become another isolated moment of confidence that feels meaningful for a week and then disappears. I’ve had those before.
So the useful lesson isn’t that anxiety has been defeated. It hasn’t. It is that being anxious and doing something anyway are perfectly capable of happening at the same time.
If something matters, discomfort alone probably shouldn’t get a veto.
And, at minimum, I now have a very good orange T-shirt.

articles.title: H2 pause for experimentation talks
articles.standfirst: A recurring discussion on experimentation opportunities has been paused until the BBC’s second-half planning position becomes clearer.

runs.text: BBC Scotland’s Pacific Quay headquarters in Glasgow. Image: OCS.
H2 pause for experimentation talks

A recurring BBC discussion on opportunities for product engineering teams to use experimentation has been cancelled for now, with the calendar note saying it can return once the outcome of second-half planning is clearer.

The change appeared on the BBC calendar for Wednesday 23 September, where a 40-minute session titled “Experimentaion for product engineering teams - opportunities” was marked cancelled. The accompanying note was unusually direct: the series is being stopped until there is greater clarity on H2 planning outcomes, with an expectation that there will be a need for it again.

It is a small diary change, but one that lands at a significant point for experimentation work. Recent months have involved a push to make experimentation easier to run across product teams, alongside work on the operating model, measurement confidence, dependencies and governance. Those themes were also central to the experimentation challenges session held on 17 September.

The pause does not amount to a cancellation of experimentation work itself. The Experiment Enablement UX stand-up remains in the BBC calendar for Friday 25 September, followed by another stand-up and a sprint review on Tuesday 29 September. That distinction matters: the regular delivery rhythm is still visible, while the wider conversation with product engineering teams is being held back pending planning decisions.

That makes the timing more interesting than the meeting title might suggest. Experimentation work has already exposed a familiar set of organisational problems: unclear ownership, handover friction, inconsistent practice, delays caused by approvals and specialist input, and difficulty establishing confidence in metrics when tools or tracking disagree. A broader opportunity discussion is most useful when teams know what they are actually trying to deliver and who has capacity to support it.

The calendar change therefore reads less like retreat and more like sequencing. Rather than continuing a recurring forum while H2 priorities are unsettled, the discussion can restart against a clearer set of commitments.

There is also a busy end to September ahead. The BBC calendar shows an Experiment Enablement sprint review on 29 September, while the DIBI conference begins at Dynamic Earth in Edinburgh on 30 September. That event has already been flagged as a useful chance to look outward at wider design and technology practice after an unusually experimentation-heavy period at work.

For now, the practical message is simple: delivery continues, but one strand of the wider experimentation conversation is on hold. What replaces it, and how quickly it returns, will depend on where the BBC’s H2 planning lands.

articles.title: Invoice ready on £150 Stereo design job
articles.standfirst: A £150 invoice for Stereo Presents marks the latest paid graphic-design commission moving from finished work to payment.

runs.text: Stereo on Renfield Lane in Glasgow city centre. Picture: Hidden Scotland.
Invoice ready on £150 Stereo design job
A PAID Glasgow design job has moved into its final, less glamorous phase: getting the invoice out the door.

A £150 bill for graphic-design work on Stereo Presents’ IPP 3 campaign was prepared on Tuesday, 22 September, marking another small but concrete piece of independent work alongside the day job at the BBC.

The invoice, numbered INV-0002, covers one graphic-design commission and is addressed to Stereo Presents CIC. A draft email with the PDF attached is ready to send, with the recipient back after an out-of-office period on 21 September.

It is not a giant agency account or a life-changing cheque. But that is precisely what makes it useful evidence of something more practical: paid creative work continuing to exist outside the main UX role, with a real client, a defined deliverable and an actual number attached to it.

Stereo itself is a long-running independent fixture in Glasgow city centre. The venue says it has operated since 2007 from its Renfield Lane home, combining a café and bar with gigs, club nights and community events. It describes itself as rooted in DIY culture, experimentation and community, and as a supporter of local and home-grown talent.

That makes the commission a neat fit with the wider strand of side work already developing around Glasgow culture and independent projects. Recent planning has also put poster-making, a possible dropship shop, England Weekend Television and exploratory Blender work into a single Notion system, an attempt to stop a growing pile of ideas competing for attention at once.

The Stereo job is different from those speculative projects because the commercial loop is already almost complete. The design work has been delivered, the fee is fixed and the paperwork exists. What remains is administration: send the email, wait for payment and close the job properly.

The £150 fee is modest, particularly against a longer-term freelance day-rate ambition of £400, but it provides a useful benchmark. Small commissions can expose the boring infrastructure that creative side work needs if it is ever to become repeatable: invoicing, contact details, payment references, file storage and a clear record of what was supplied.

There is also a timing advantage. Wednesday’s BBC calendar has a busy start, including a 09:00 Account Epic Review, but the recurring experimentation opportunities session later in the morning has been cancelled while H2 planning becomes clearer. That leaves more space later in the day to close loose ends rather than open another project.
For now, the headline is simple. The work is done. The invoice is ready. The next milestone is money in the bank.

articles.title: Five projects, one place
articles.standfirst: A new Notion hub will bring posters, money, Blender, England Weekend Television and outreach into one manageable plan.

runs.text: Notion will become the central hub for a new personal project system. Image: Notion Labs/Wikimedia Commons
Five projects, one place
A sprawling list of creative ambitions is being pulled into one system after a push to turn a busy mix of side projects into something that can actually be managed.

The new setup will use Notion as a central hub for five live strands: an ongoing poster practice and possible dropship shop, a personal finances reset, experiments in Blender, further work on England Weekend Television, and a plan to cold-call photographer Ed Campbell.

The move follows a blunt problem: there is plenty to do, but no single place showing what matters now, what can wait and what the next action actually is. Rather than treating every idea as equally urgent, the plan is to give each project a home, a status and a clear next step.

It is a small bit of admin with a bigger purpose. The poster work is intended to continue in the background while a route to selling prints through dropshipping is explored. Money needs its own practical track rather than competing for attention with creative work. Blender, meanwhile, is deliberately being kept playful, with room for experiments to grow into something more substantial without forcing a commercial outcome too early.

England Weekend Television remains a separate active project, with further development planned alongside direct outreach to Ed Campbell. The point is not to cram all of that into one week. It is to stop the projects becoming a single undifferentiated cloud of things that ought to be happening.

Notion is a fairly natural fit for that job. The company describes the product as a connected workspace combining documents, projects and databases, and its project tools support tasks, dependencies and custom properties. That makes it possible to keep a lightweight portfolio view while still giving each strand its own notes and actions.

The wider shift is from remembering projects to running them. A dashboard can show the handful of things currently moving, while ideas that are not active can stay visible without demanding immediate attention.

That matters because the aim is not maximum productivity for its own sake. The mix includes commercial work, personal housekeeping and things being done simply because they are interesting. A useful system has to preserve that distinction rather than turn every hobby into another job.

The immediate result is simple: five projects now have a prospective common home, and the next phase is to turn the list into a working rhythm rather than another beautifully organised graveyard of intentions.

articles.title: Government marks tremendous victory in new approach to discomfort
articles.standfirst: A successful visit to the Get Glasgow Moving exhibition will form the starting point for a wider approach to anxiety, participation and doing things that matter.

runs.text: Government marks tremendous victory in new approach to discomfort
Government for SwS marks a new approach to discomfort following a visit to the Get Glasgow Moving anniversary exhibition.
The Government for SwS has today celebrated a tremendous victory following a successful solo visit to the Get Glasgow Moving 10-year anniversary exhibition at the New Glasgow Society.

The visit followed considerable anticipatory anxiety about attending the exhibition alone, entering an unfamiliar social environment and potentially encountering people involved with an organisation in which Sam has a longstanding interest.
Despite this, Sam attended the exhibition, viewed the work, briefly interacted with staff and purchased an orange Get Glasgow Moving T-shirt.
The Government considers the apparently routine visit significant because it provides further evidence that anticipatory anxiety is a poor predictor of Sam’s experience once an activity has begun.
A new approach to discomfort
Following the visit, the Government has set out a developing principle for future personal and professional decisions:
Comfort is useful infrastructure, but a bad decision-maker.
The Government will not pursue discomfort for its own sake, nor abandon routines, systems or accommodations that make everyday life easier.
Instead, where an opportunity is important to Sam and anxiety is the principal reason for avoiding it, greater weight will be given to the underlying desire to participate.
This will particularly apply to opportunities involving community participation, public speaking, professional development, creative work and involvement in Glasgow’s civic and cultural life.

The objective is not to eliminate anticipatory anxiety before taking action. Instead, the Government will support a longer-term shift towards becoming comfortable with being uncomfortable and developing greater confidence in Sam’s ability to act while anxious.
From observation to participation
The Get Glasgow Moving exhibition is also significant because of Sam’s longer-term interest in becoming involved with the organisation and contributing more directly to positive change in Glasgow.
During the exhibition, Sam concluded that there was no fundamental reason why he could not eventually become part of spaces such as this.

The Government recognises that previous successful experiences have not always resulted in sustained behavioural change. Periods of increased confidence have sometimes been followed by months without further action.
The next phase will therefore focus on converting individual successes into continued participation rather than treating them as isolated achievements.
Success will not require Sam to become naturally extroverted, eliminate anxiety or perform confidently in every unfamiliar situation.
If something matters, discomfort alone is not a veto.
Today’s visit represents the first practical demonstration of that approach.
The orange T-shirt will be retained as evidence of the tremendous victory.

articles.title: Sagging has become the default at home
articles.standfirst: Sagging has shifted from an outward styling choice to an everyday default at home, revealing a clearer boundary between private comfort, personal presentation, family and work.

runs.text: Image: Sagging trousers at Tate Modern, London, 2010. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Gaywash (CC BY-SA 2.0).
Sagging has become the default at home
Something has changed in the relationship between SwS and sagging. What was once mainly a way of dressing outside the home has become the default even when nobody else is around.

At the family home, sagging tended to stop at the front door. Trousers might be worn low while out, but at home they were pulled back up. Living independently has removed that distinction. The waistband is now routinely visible while relaxing around the flat and the habit can continue into bed. It no longer needs an occasion, an outfit or another person to see it.

The remaining boundaries are revealing. Sagging is still generally switched off around family and at work, where a different standard of presentation takes over. Elsewhere, the low waistband has increasingly become the neutral position rather than a deliberate styling decision made each time.

That does not necessarily need a grand psychological explanation. Repetition can turn a chosen look into something familiar and automatic. But the change is still useful to notice: sagging now appears to function as part of personal presentation even in private, rather than only as a signal sent to other people.

There is also a stronger sense of ownership in being able to dress this way at home. The move from a family home, where the style was compartmentalised, to a private space where it does not need to be moderated has allowed it to become more continuous. The distinction is less between public and private than between environments where the style feels available and those where it does not.

Recent conversations have pushed that observation further, including the question of what it means psychologically when a clothing habit persists with no audience at all. The most defensible conclusion is fairly simple: the behaviour has become normalised enough that its private continuation now feels unremarkable. Anything more specific about motive would be speculation.

That interest also produced the deliberately niche sag-score app concept developed on Monday. The idea of using an iPhone camera and depth sensing to measure how low trousers are sitting is less the main story than a consequence of paying unusually close attention to the habit. Quantifying the drop turns something intuitive into something observable.

For now, there is no new rule or policy around sagging. The useful record is the change itself: a style once associated mainly with going out has become part of everyday life at home, while clear boundaries around family and work remain.

articles.title: DIBI countdown begins
articles.standfirst: With DIBI 2026 just eight days away, attention turns to two days of practical product design and technology thinking at Dynamic Earth.

runs.text: DIBI conference branding at an earlier event. Image: HeadBox / The Biscuit Room.
DIBI countdown begins
DIBI is heading back to Edinburgh next week, with the two-day digital product and technology conference due to open at Dynamic Earth on Wednesday 30 September.

The event, which runs into Thursday 1 October, bills itself around “actionable insights for product people” and brings design, development and product thinking together rather than treating them as separate disciplines. For a UX practice increasingly concerned with experimentation, evidence and how design operates inside wider product systems, that makes this year’s programme particularly well timed.

DIBI says its speakers are intended to inform, challenge and inspire across commercial, creative and technical domains. Product designer Joel Miller of Figma is among the names currently promoted by organisers, while Herb Kim is returning as host. Alongside the talks, the conference includes practical workshops and networking across the two days.

The timing lands during a busy stretch of design work. The BBC calendar shows Experiment Enablement UX stand-ups continuing this week, alongside a Data UX check-in today and an Account Epic Review on Wednesday. A separate session on opportunities for experimentation in product engineering teams has been cancelled pending clearer H2 planning outcomes, a small but telling reminder that the organisational conditions around experimentation remain in motion.

That context matters. Recent experimentation work has repeatedly surfaced questions about ownership, measurement confidence, governance and the point at which specialist input enters the process. DIBI’s broad product-and-tech framing offers a useful chance to look beyond individual UX methods and towards how design decisions survive contact with engineering, commercial constraints and organisational reality.

There is also a strong practical streak to the event. Organisers promise workshops built around tools, techniques and ideas that attendees can apply directly in their roles. That emphasis should help separate the conference from the familiar circuit of inspirational design talks that sound good on stage but struggle to make it into Monday morning’s work.
Dynamic Earth will host the conference again, placing the event beside Holyrood in central Edinburgh. Conference passes are currently advertised at £255 excluding VAT.

With eight days to go, the interesting question is less whether DIBI can produce another round of polished product talks and more whether its mix of design, development and business thinking can offer anything genuinely useful for the messier work now happening around experimentation.
For
SWS.GOV
, that is the bit worth watching.

articles.title: Two minutes, one button, one tiny Pi
articles.standfirst: A pocket-sized Raspberry Pi device could turn a single button press into a two-minute timer backed by a randomly selected local audio track.

runs.text: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. Image: Raspberry Pi Ltd
Two minutes, one button, one tiny Pi

A new pocket-sized hardware idea could turn a single physical button into a deliberately simple two-minute ritual: press it, start a timer and hear one randomly chosen two-minute audio track from a local library.

The concept, explored on Monday night, is deliberately narrower than most smart-device projects. Rather than adding a screen full of controls or relying on a phone, the proposed machine would do one thing immediately. A button press would trigger a two-minute countdown while a small speaker plays a randomly selected recording stored on the device itself.

The current plan is for a battery-operated build based around Raspberry Pi hardware, with a physical push button, local audio storage and a compact speaker. That keeps the core interaction self-contained and avoids needing a network connection once the audio library has been loaded.

A Raspberry Pi Zero-class board is a plausible fit for that brief. The current Zero 2 W measures just 65mm by 30mm and combines a 1GHz quad-core processor with a microSD slot and a 40-pin GPIO header footprint, giving a small enclosure enough computing power to handle audio playback, timing and button input without the bulk of a full-size computer.

Raspberry Pi itself describes the Zero 2 W as suitable for embedded projects including Bluetooth speakers and other small connected devices. For this build, though, the attraction is less about connectivity than physicality. The useful bit is the ability to wire a real button into GPIO and make the interaction instant and predictable.

The software could remain equally lean. On startup, the Pi would wait for a button event. Once pressed, it would choose an audio file at random, begin playback and run the two-minute timer in parallel. At the end, playback stops and the machine returns to its waiting state. A simple lockout would prevent repeated presses from starting overlapping sessions.

There are still hardware decisions to make. Battery capacity, amplifier choice, speaker size, charging circuitry and the enclosure will determine whether the finished object feels like a neat handheld product or a desk-bound prototype. A smaller microcontroller could potentially handle an even more stripped-back version, but a Pi offers an easier route for managing a changing local playlist and ordinary audio files.

The idea also marks a shift from recent screen-heavy personal projects towards a deliberately tangible bit of interaction design. The experience is defined by one control, one fixed duration and a small element of surprise. There is no account, feed or menu to navigate.
That constraint is the point. Two minutes in, the device is finished with you until the next press.

articles.title: Ten years of Get Glasgow Moving
articles.standfirst: A ten-year exhibition charts how a grassroots Glasgow transport campaign moved from protest to the brink of bus franchising and Clyde Metro.

runs.text: Image: Buchanan Bus Station in Glasgow, photographed in July 2026. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Richard Sutcliffe (CC BY-SA 2.0).
Ten years of Get Glasgow Moving

A Glasgow transport campaign that began with a group of local people in 2016 is marking its first decade with an exhibition tracing ten years of pressure for a simpler, more integrated public transport system.

Get Glasgow Moving’s 10th Anniversary Exhibition is running at the New Glasgow Society on Argyle Street from 18 to 23 September, opening daily from noon until 17:00. The show looks back at the campaign’s wins and setbacks since its launch a decade ago and places that history against a much bigger question: how close Glasgow now is to the kind of joined-up network campaigners have spent years demanding.

The timing is sharp. Get Glasgow Moving says the region is now on the cusp of major change through Strathclyde Partnership for Transport’s work on bus franchising and the longer-term Clyde Metro programme. Those projects are not finished deals, and their eventual shape still matters, but they represent a markedly different transport landscape from the one the campaign entered in September 2016.
For
SWS.GOV

, the exhibition lands squarely in familiar territory. Glasgow’s fragmented transport system, the balance between public control and private operation, and the way streets and networks shape everyday life have all become recurring interests. A Sunday trip into town has now put the anniversary exhibition on the agenda as a compact bit of transport history rather than another abstract policy debate.

The campaign’s story is useful precisely because it joins those two levels together. Bus regulation can sound procedural. Integration can sound like a diagram. But the practical argument is much simpler: whether a passenger can move around Greater Glasgow without having to think about competing operators, disconnected tickets or a network whose parts do not always behave like one system.

That is also why the anniversary arrives at an interesting point politically. The exhibition describes bus franchising and Clyde Metro as routes towards a world-class integrated system, while its retrospective format makes clear that the present position took years of campaigning rather than appearing overnight. The launch event on 17 September brought together activists involved in the campaign’s early years to discuss that journey.

The New Glasgow Society exhibition is free to visit and does not require booking. Its Argyle Street location also makes the subject feel appropriately embedded in the city it is arguing about, rather than sealed off in a transport conference or policy document.

Ten years on, the campaign has not reached an end point. But an exhibition built around a decade of pressure offers a useful chance to see how far Glasgow’s transport debate has shifted, and how much of the original case for change is now moving from campaigning language into actual plans.

articles.title: One more year of a third off
articles.standfirst: A £35 renewal will keep a third off most rail fares for another year as the current 26–30 Railcard enters its final month.

runs.text: Image: a ScotRail Class 385 at Glasgow Central. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by TriStateGuy.
One more year of a third off
The countdown is on for another year of cheaper train travel, with the current 26–30 Railcard due to expire on 16 October and the renewal window already open.

The simplest route is also the obvious one: renew the existing digital Railcard through the official Railcard account. The 26–30 card costs £35 for one year and cuts a third from most eligible rail fares across Great Britain. There is no three-year version, so there is little scope for clever shopping around here.

Official Railcard guidance says renewals can be made up to 30 days before expiry. That means the 16 October card is now comfortably inside the renewal window. For a digital Railcard bought online, renewal can be completed through the existing account and generally does not require another eligibility check.

The current card already lives in the official Railcard app, making continuity fairly painless. Once the replacement is ready, the digital card can be added to the phone rather than waiting for anything to arrive through the post.

At £35, the maths remains fairly forgiving. Railcard says the 26–30 version saves holders a third on train tickets and estimates average annual savings of £283 after the cost of the card, based on journeys made between April 2025 and March 2026. The precise saving will obviously depend on how much rail travel actually happens over the next year.

There are some restrictions worth remembering. A £12 minimum fare normally applies to journeys made between 04:30 and 09:59 from Monday to Friday, although Advance fares and public holidays are exempt. The card covers Standard Anytime, Off-Peak, Super Off-Peak and Advance tickets, with First Class Advance also included.

The timing also removes any age-related complication. A 26–30 Railcard can be bought while the holder is aged 26 to 30 and then used for its full one-year validity. With the existing card expiring next month, renewal is available now rather than requiring a switch to another product.

There is therefore no benefit in letting the current card lapse and creating a gap in discounted travel. The practical job is small: sign into the existing Railcard account, renew for £35 before 16 October, then make sure the new digital card is active in the app before using a discounted ticket after the old one expires.

It is hardly the most dramatic bit of Government business, but it is exactly the sort of boring admin that becomes expensive when ignored. One payment keeps the familiar one-third discount running for another year, with no new card to carry and no reason to leave it until the final day.

articles.title: Old iPad eyed for SWS.GOV kiosk
articles.standfirst: A search for a cheap full-screen iPad has opened up a simple route to giving SWS.GOV a dedicated always-on kiosk display.

runs.text: Image: iPad (10th generation). Source: Wikimedia Commons, image by Riski394.
Old iPad eyed for
SWS.GOV
kiosk
A cheap second-hand iPad is being considered for a new job inside the
SWS.GOV
setup: a dedicated full-screen kiosk for the growing personal dashboard.

The idea emerged from a deliberately narrow hardware search this week. The requirement is not for a powerful tablet, a laptop replacement or another general-purpose device. It needs to run a web browser, lose the old physical Home button and present a modern edge-to-edge screen that can sit permanently on the
SWS.GOV
experience.

That makes older full-screen iPads unusually well suited to the brief. Apple’s tenth-generation iPad, released in October 2022, was the first standard iPad to adopt the flatter modern design without a Home button. It also moved the base model to USB-C, making permanent power and mounting simpler than on older Lightning-based models.

Apple still lists the tenth-generation model among iPads using USB-C. The model has since been replaced by the newer A16 iPad, leaving the older hardware as the more interesting target for a used-device search rather than a new purchase.
The important bit is what the screen would actually do. Project Indigo has been pushing
SWS.GOV

away from being a collection of pages and towards something closer to a personal operating dashboard. The redesigned homepage is intended to surface useful information, services and Government material in one place, while universal search reaches across the SWS archive, Google and the
SWS.GOV
ChatGPT project.
Putting that interface on a dedicated device changes the proposition slightly. Instead of
SWS.GOV
being something opened deliberately in a browser, it could become an ambient display: always available, immediately glanceable and separate from the phone or main computer.

That is why performance is not the priority. A kiosk does not need the latest processor, large storage capacity or premium cameras. Browser support, a clean full-screen display, reliable Wi-Fi and the ability to remain powered are the useful bits. Buying used also makes more sense for hardware expected to spend most of its life attached to a stand or wall rather than carried around.

There are still practical details to settle. A suitable second-hand model has not yet been bought, and the final setup would need a secure mount, sensible charging arrangement and a browser configuration that keeps the interface on screen without unnecessary controls getting in the way.
The hardware search nevertheless gives Project Indigo a possible physical endpoint. The redesign has so far concentrated on making
SWS.GOV
more personal and useful on the web. A cheap retired iPad could turn that same interface into a small piece of infrastructure in the flat.

articles.title: The buzz is back at GCU
articles.standfirst: A two-hour Masters introduction at Glasgow Caledonian University ended on a high as presenting familiar design material delivered an unexpected Friday buzz.

runs.text: Glasgow Caledonian University campus. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Knwwsss.
The buzz is back at GCU

A Friday afternoon presentation at Glasgow Caledonian University has turned a carefully prepared return to the classroom into something more immediate: a reminder that talking about design can be genuinely good fun.

The Masters week-one introduction ran from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday 18 September, according to the BBC calendar. It was the surviving half of a two-session plan after the earlier introduction was cancelled, making the afternoon the first proper chance to deliver the material to students.

Preparation had been deliberately light by the time the session arrived. After one run through the presenter notes, the material already felt familiar enough to avoid grinding through repeated rehearsals. The calculation was simple: the subject matter was known, the structure was understood and over-rehearsing risked making the delivery stiffer rather than better.

That approach paid off. Once the presentation was finished, the verdict was emphatic: it had been fun, with a particular buzz coming from presenting something already understood well enough to speak about naturally rather than simply reading a script.

The session drew on practical design thinking rather than treating UX as a procession of screens. One exercise asked students to design a doorbell, a prompt that predictably encourages a rectangle with a button. The brief then shifts to the actual need: design a way of knowing somebody is at the door. The change is small, but it opens the problem up and demonstrates why designers need to separate a user need from the first obvious solution.

The presentation also tackled generative AI, now difficult to avoid in a design course in 2026. The emphasis was on responsible use: AI can help explore ideas, accelerate parts of a design process and support more complex prototyping, but it should complement rather than replace design thinking. Privacy, safe tooling, checking outputs and being transparent about its use remain part of the job.

For SwS, the more interesting outcome came after the slides were done. Presenting is not a routine part of every working day, but the afternoon reinforced a useful distinction between nerves caused by unfamiliarity and the energy that comes from explaining a subject with genuine command of it.

That matters beyond one university session. Recent work has involved research synthesis, experimentation practice and explaining complex design processes to different audiences. Being able to turn that knowledge into a clear story is increasingly part of the design work itself, not an extra task bolted on afterwards.

The GCU appearance therefore closes the week on a different note from the planning that preceded it. What began as another item in the calendar ended as a fairly strong argument for doing more of this sort of thing: know the material, keep the structure clear, then get up and talk about it.

articles.title: Project Indigo redraws SWS.GOV
articles.standfirst: A beta overhaul introduces a personalised dashboard, universal search and a new design language as SWS.GOV begins its biggest rebuild yet.

runs.text: Glasgow City Chambers, a suitably governmental backdrop for the latest
SWS.GOV
rebuild. Source: Wikimedia Commons.
Project Indigo redraws
SWS.GOV
SWS.GOV
has begun its biggest visual and functional overhaul yet, with the new Project Indigo experience now in beta and a markedly different idea of what the Government’s digital front door should do.

The rebuild centres on a redesigned homepage that behaves less like a conventional government landing page and more like a personal dashboard. Information is intended to be more useful at a glance, with stronger personalisation and quicker routes into the services, records and tools that matter day to day.
It is also a deliberate break from the site’s earlier look.
SWS.GOV

has long borrowed heavily from the visual language established by the UK Government Digital Service. Project Indigo keeps the same underlying commitment to clarity, accessibility and straightforward interaction, but moves towards a more distinctive modernist digital design language of its own.

That means redesigned components across the site, with new typography, colour, depth and animation being introduced as individual areas are rebuilt. The change is being rolled out progressively rather than through a single big-bang replacement, allowing older sections to remain available while their Indigo versions are completed.
Search is one of the more ambitious parts of the beta. A new universal search experience is designed to work across the
SWS.GOV
archive while also opening routes into Google and the dedicated
SWS.GOV
ChatGPT project. The aim is to make search less of a simple list of site results and more of a common starting point for finding, researching or asking for something.
The News experience has also been rebuilt. That work lands alongside a wider shift in how
SWS.GOV

content is produced, with Google Docs now acting as the canonical source for structured articles and publishing metadata. The new front end is therefore arriving at the same time as the machinery behind it is becoming more formal and reliable.
Project Indigo also marks a change in the Government’s approach to AI. Existing AI features built directly into
SWS.GOV

, including the article-writing tool, are being deprecated. Rather than maintaining separate lightweight AI features on the site, the direction now is towards closer integration with ChatGPT itself, where the broader Government for SwS context and archive can be used more effectively.

That distinction matters. The earlier approach treated AI as a feature added to individual pages. Indigo instead treats it as part of the wider information architecture, sitting alongside search, the archive and the dashboard rather than competing with them.
The rest of
SWS.GOV

will now be rebuilt piece by piece around the same principles. Planned and emerging areas include a redesigned Archive, Planner and Recipes experience, alongside the continuing conversion of existing pages to the new component system.
There is no single switch-over date for the whole site. For now, Project Indigo remains a beta running alongside the older experience. But the direction is settled: the previous
SWS.GOV
established the system; Indigo is intended to turn it into a genuinely useful personal operating surface.

articles.title: The farm hiding beside Cumbernauld’s motorway
articles.standfirst: A look at Mainhead Farm and the roads around Westerwood has opened a new line of inquiry into the landscape Cumbernauld’s New Town inherited.

runs.text: Mainhead Farm, now home to Caulders Cumbernauld. Image: Caulders Garden Centres.
The farm hiding beside Cumbernauld’s motorway
A garden centre beside one of Cumbernauld’s busiest junctions has become the starting point for a deeper look at what survived when the New Town arrived.

Caulders Cumbernauld sits at Mainhead Farm beside Westerwood Roundabout, just off the M80. The business itself is a relatively recent occupant: Caulders says it took over the Cumbernauld centre in 2019 and has since expanded its plant area, restaurant and shop. But the site name points to an older layer of the landscape that is easy to miss among the motorway slips, roundabouts and industrial roads.
The question now being explored is how much of the road pattern around Mainhead predates the New Town, and how much was imposed as Cumbernauld expanded north and west.

That distinction matters because Cumbernauld was not built on empty ground. The town was designated in December 1955, but existing farms, villages and routes were already spread across the area. The original New Town was later enlarged north of the old A80, with Westfield, Balloch, Westerwood and Carrickstone among the areas brought into the planned expansion.

Wardpark adds another clue. The industrial estate became a major employment zone during the New Town era, and its road connections were necessarily important to the developing town. The former Burroughs factory there is recorded as the first factory of the Cumbernauld New Town. That makes the route towards Wardpark an obvious candidate for comparing pre-development roads with the infrastructure created for the planned town.

Carrickstone tells a slightly different story. Modern housing came later, but the name is much older. Historic mapping records Carrickstone Farm, while the area is associated with the Carrick Stone, the Roman altar that remains in the open air. The result is a familiar Cumbernauld pattern: a modern neighbourhood carrying forward a name from the rural landscape it replaced.

Mainhead now looks particularly interesting because the garden centre still presents itself using the farm name. Its address is officially Mainhead Farm, Westerwood Roundabout, Cumbernauld, G68 0EB. The surviving stonework visible around the centre also raises the obvious question of whether parts of the present complex belong to an earlier farm building, although that has not yet been established from a reliable historic source.

The next stage is therefore less about guessing from architecture and more about maps. Comparing Ordnance Survey sheets from before 1955 with New Town plans and later aerial photography should show which alignments were retained, diverted or erased as the A80, Wardpark and the western neighbourhoods developed.

It is a small investigation, but a revealing one. Cumbernauld is usually read through its modernist architecture and post-war planning. Around Westerwood, the older landscape may still be sitting in plain sight, encoded in a farm name, a bend in a road and the routes that the New Town chose not to wipe away.

articles.title: GCU teaching return puts design challenge in focus
articles.standfirst: A return to Glasgow Caledonian University will put professional UX practice in front of Masters students as a new design project gets under way.

runs.text: Image: Glasgow Caledonian University campus in Glasgow. Source: Study UK, British Council.
GCU teaching return puts design challenge in focus
A return to Glasgow Caledonian University is set to put day-to-day professional UX practice directly in front of Masters students, as a new design project begins on Friday.

The two-hour introduction, scheduled for 15:00 to 17:00 on 18 September, marks another step in SwS’s growing involvement with teaching and industry outreach. The session is intended to introduce the design project to Masters students and follows earlier planning with Kevin around how to turn real design practice into a useful student challenge.

The timing is notable. SwS joined the BBC through its UX trainee route in 2022 after studying at Glasgow Caledonian, and has since moved through junior and midweight design roles into the Data and Experimentation Enablement team. Returning to the university therefore brings the route back round: recent professional experience is now becoming material for students beginning their own advanced design work.

The planned challenge is built around an everyday object rather than a grand speculative brief. A doorbell provides the starting point, giving students something immediately understandable while opening up harder questions about users, context, accessibility, behaviour and the consequences of adding technology to an apparently simple interaction.

That simplicity is useful. A doorbell has a clear basic job, but designing one well means thinking beyond the button itself. Who is arriving? Who is inside? What happens if someone cannot hear it, reach it or respond immediately? What information should be captured, and what should not? Once cameras, recognition systems, notifications or AI enter the picture, the design problem quickly becomes as much about judgement as interface craft.

The teaching plan is expected to use those tensions to push students beyond producing a polished screen. Ethics and AI form part of the wider discussion, with the emphasis on asking whether a capability should be used and what trade-offs it creates, rather than treating new technology as an automatic improvement.

That approach closely matches the work SwS has been doing at the BBC. Recent experimentation research has focused less on isolated interface problems and more on the systems around them: ownership, evidence, dependencies, governance and the points where apparently local decisions create effects elsewhere. The university session applies the same kind of thinking in a different setting.

Friday is already marked as a non-working day on the BBC calendar, with an out-of-office block from midday, clearing the afternoon for the university session. A first version of the introduction had appeared on Thursday’s calendar before being cancelled and replaced by the Friday slot.

The result is a small but meaningful expansion of the work beyond the BBC. Rather than presenting UX as a set of methods or portfolio conventions, the session has the chance to show design as the messier practice it actually is: framing problems, making choices with incomplete information and being able to explain why a decision is responsible.
For SwS, it is also a return to familiar ground with a rather different role. The next visit to GCU is not about being a student. It is about helping set the problem.

articles.title: GCU teaching return moves to Friday
articles.standfirst: A planned first Masters introduction at Glasgow Caledonian University was cancelled on Thursday, leaving Friday’s second session as the new start for the design teaching return.

GCU teaching return moves to Friday

The BBC calendar had originally shown a two-hour session at the Cowcaddens campus from 13:00 on Thursday 17 September, but that entry is now marked cancelled. A second session remains in place for Friday 18 September from 15:00 to 17:00, described as the second of two sessions introducing the design project to Masters students.

The change is a small scheduling move, but a meaningful update to plans set out earlier this week. The teaching return had been prepared around a practical design challenge developed with Kevin, using the everyday problem of a doorbell as a route into broader questions about design decisions, ethics and the growing role of AI.

That work is intended to be more than a conventional guest lecture. The challenge gives students a deliberately ordinary object and asks them to think through the people, systems and consequences around it. The aim is to move quickly from an apparently simple interface problem into the messier territory that sits behind real product design.

Friday’s session will also mark a return to familiar ground. SwS studied at Glasgow Caledonian before leaving during the final year to join the BBC, and has since returned as a guest contributor. The university’s Glasgow operation remains a single-site city campus at Cowcaddens, where undergraduate and postgraduate teaching is concentrated within walking distance of the city centre.

The timing now sits alongside a non-working day on the BBC calendar. An out-of-office block begins at noon on Friday, before the GCU session starts at 15:00. That creates a cleaner break between BBC work and the university commitment than Thursday’s original arrangement would have allowed.

Thursday itself remains busy. A morning web experimentation session focused on self-service, targeting, assignment, tracking and measurement was followed by the wider UX&D Studio Day from 13:00. The cancelled GCU introduction would have overlapped directly with that three-hour cross-location event.

The revised plan therefore leaves the teaching work with a more distinct slot of its own. There is no indication in the calendar that Friday’s session has been cancelled or moved, so it remains the confirmed next step at the time of writing.

The substance of the project has not changed. The task is still to introduce Masters students to a design problem that can open out into questions of responsibility, technology and human judgement, rather than simply teaching a set of interface techniques.
For
SWS.GOV
