articles.title: Experimentation Day puts web challenges in focus
articles.standfirst: A BBC-wide Experimentation Day has put evidence-led decision making centre stage as SwS prepares to test months of workflow research against the practical challenges of experimenting on the web.

runs.text: Image: BBC Scotland at Pacific Quay in Glasgow. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Batchelor.
Experimentation Day puts web challenges in focus

A BBC-wide day focused on experimentation has landed at a useful moment for SwS, as months of work mapping how experiments actually happen moves towards a sharper test against the problems teams face on the web.

Experimentation Day 2026 ran from 10:00 to 15:30 on Wednesday 16 September, with a programme built around understanding users and making better decisions. The internal event brought together keynote talks, BBC lightning talks, roundtable discussions and a closing session on decision making.

For SwS, the timing is unusually neat. The current rotation in experimentation has spent recent months examining the end-to-end journey from IDEATE through PLAN, BUILD, TEST, DECIDE and LEARN, with research repeatedly surfacing friction around ownership, measurement confidence, dependencies and governance.

The emerging picture is not simply that experiments are technically difficult. Earlier problems can accumulate across the process. Unclear ownership and inconsistent involvement at the start can lead to gaps later, while uncertainty around measurement can make teams less confident in the evidence they have. By the time an experiment reaches a decision, unresolved issues can increase the need for deeper analysis and specialist input before a conclusion can be reached.

That work now has an immediate next test. The BBC calendar shows a one-hour session on Thursday morning titled “Challenges in Expeirmentation Web”, intended to capture and validate where web experimentation is slow, complex or dependent on specialist support.

Its scope runs across the full workflow, from identifying an opportunity through setup, targeting and activation to measurement and analysis. The session is also due to examine where teams cannot self-serve, limitations around signed-in and signed-out identity, targeting and segmentation, assignment and tracking, and gaps in the metrics available for analysis.

That makes Thursday less of a fresh discovery exercise and more of a chance to pressure-test the wider operating-model findings against a specific platform. The strongest opportunity is to see whether the same structural problems found across experimentation show up in web delivery, and where the web introduces genuinely different constraints.

The distinction matters. Recent synthesis has increasingly moved away from isolated pain points towards a connected account of how the system behaves. Measurement consistency, for example, is not only an analytics concern if weak confidence in data later forces additional review. Governance is not only a final sign-off issue if missing input earlier creates the need for specialist voices at the end.

The calendar also points to a busy day around the session, with an Experiment Enablement UX stand-up beforehand and the wider UX&D Studio Day beginning at 13:00. The web discussion, however, is the clearest continuation of the current experimentation work.

After several months spent turning interviews, process maps and research synthesis into a usable view of the problem, the next step is increasingly concrete: establish which problems are shared, which are web-specific, and where better enablement could remove friction without simply moving it elsewhere.

articles.title: Oasis cinema trip caps music-heavy day
articles.standfirst: A Glasgow cinema trip to see Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger rounds off a day dominated by the band’s return to the spotlight.

runs.text: Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger. Image: film poster. Source: The FADER.
Oasis cinema trip caps music-heavy day
A trip into Glasgow for Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger is set to round off a day in which the Manchester band has been difficult to escape.

The 2026 documentary, directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, follows Liam and Noel Gallagher through the Oasis Live ’25 reunion tour. The film combines rehearsal, backstage and onstage footage with the brothers’ first joint interviews in more than 20 years, turning last year’s comeback into a two-hour cinema account of one of the biggest music stories of 2025.

The Glasgow screening is due to finish at 22:59 on Tuesday 15 September. With the film itself running for 123 minutes, the feature is expected to begin at roughly 20:56, after the usual cinema advertising and trailers. Travel planning earlier in the evening centred on getting from Mount Florida into Glasgow Central with enough time to spare rather than cutting the journey fine.

Several trains offered workable options. A 19:35 departure from Mount Florida, arriving at Glasgow Central at 19:45, provided a particularly comfortable margin before the advertised cinema time, while later services remained possible. The exercise was a small but familiar bit of logistics: work backwards from the actual likely film start, then decide how much hanging around in town is preferable to the risk of arriving late.

The film itself arrived in UK cinemas this month after the extraordinary scale of the Oasis reunion. It documents the Live ’25 tour, which brought Liam and Noel back onto the same stage after the band’s 2009 split. Official cinema material describes the documentary as an account not just of the performances but of the emotional impact of the comeback across generations of fans.

That makes the screening more than a straightforward concert film. The reunion was already one of the defining popular-culture events of last year, while Don’t Look Back In Anger packages the rehearsals, performances and renewed Gallagher partnership into a permanent record of it.

The cinema trip also lands amid another burst of Oasis activity. The band remains firmly back in the cultural conversation rather than existing purely as a 1990s concern, with the documentary extending the comeback beyond the stadium shows and into cinemas.

For SwS, the attraction is simpler. Oasis have remained part of the regular music rotation, and a big-screen documentary offers the sort of concentrated music-and-film night that streaming at home does not quite reproduce.

Barring any last-minute change of plan, the evening therefore ends in a cinema rather than on the sofa. After working out train times, running times and the difference between the advertised screening and the probable feature start, there is only one part left: actually watching the thing.

articles.title: Cowgate short film takes shape
articles.standfirst: A woodland visit has developed into Cowgate, a short film project rooted in childhood geography and deliberately small-scale production.

runs.text: Image: Woodland near Cumbernauld. Source: Geograph Britain and Ireland.
Cowgate short film takes shape

A return to woodland around Cumbernauld has turned into a new creative project, with Cowgate now taking shape as a short film built around memory, place and the strange gap between childhood geography and adult reality.

The project emerged from a visit to a wooded area near the Whitelees estate, where an old railway alignment and steep slopes provided the setting for a compact story. The script follows Sam returning to a spot he remembers from years earlier, initially struggling to identify the right opening through vegetation that has become considerably more overgrown.

That search is the engine of the opening sequence. The character walks, stops, doubles back and eventually recognises the route before pushing through the trees and attempting the descent. At the bottom, a barbed-wire fence provides the first physical reminder that the place has changed since childhood.

The film then pushes the premise into comedy. Gavin, Jack and Johnny enter the story, with Johnny eventually discovered in an absurd state after apparently being missing at Cowgate since 2021. The script deliberately mixes recognisable local geography and conversational Glasgow humour with a ridiculous time-gap payoff.

Development has moved quickly beyond a loose idea. A full scene has been drafted, visual storyboard work has begun and poster concepts have already been explored using character and location references. That makes Cowgate a more concrete production prospect than the quick woodland-film exercise that prompted it.

The location is central rather than incidental. Cumbernauld is unusually rich in wooded corridors, a legacy partly tied to the New Town’s extensive green-space planning. The Wildlife Trusts describes Cumbernauld Glen as ancient woodland used by walkers, cyclists and horse riders, while the Woodland Trust records the nearby Glencryan Woodland at more than 57 hectares. The wider landscape gives a small production access to paths, slopes, dense vegetation and infrastructure without requiring a constructed set.

That also suits the intended scale. Cowgate is not currently being treated as a large production with an elaborate crew or effects pipeline. The appeal is that much of its character can come from the real environment, a small cast and dialogue that sounds deliberately ordinary even as the situation becomes increasingly stupid.

The project also sits alongside a separate recent idea to recreate Cumbernauld as a free-roam game. Both use the town less as generic scenery and more as source material, drawing on remembered routes, overlooked infrastructure and places that carry meaning precisely because they are mundane.

No filming date or completed production plan has yet been confirmed. The significant change is that the idea now has a title, a developed script, a defined location language and an emerging visual identity. What started as a question about what could be filmed quickly in the woods has become a short film with a recognisable shape of its own.

articles.title: Cumbernauld game plan takes shape
articles.standfirst: SwS has begun turning a long-held idea to recreate Cumbernauld as a free-roam game into a practical Blender and Unity project.

runs.text: Cumbernauld Town Centre in 1963. Image: MIT DOME.
Cumbernauld game plan takes shape
A long-held plan to recreate Cumbernauld as a free-roaming game world has moved a step closer to becoming a practical project, with Blender and Unity emerging as the likely route for building it.
The idea resurfaced during work this weekend on tools for sculpting landscapes, importing 3D models and creating explorable environments without having to hand-code an entire game from scratch.

The ambition is deliberately bigger than a static architectural model. The concept discussed would allow Cumbernauld to be rebuilt as a functioning virtual town, with roads, buildings, interiors and public transport all potentially added over time. Buses, cars, trains and even underground systems were among the elements considered possible using pre-made assets, custom Blender models and AI-assisted coding.
It revives what was described as a childhood dream of having “The Simpsons: Hit & Run in Cumbernauld”, but with modern tools making the prospect considerably less far-fetched than it once was.

The immediate route would be to create the base geography and key landmarks first, rather than attempting the whole town in one go. Terrain could be sculpted, selected buildings modelled in Blender and the pieces assembled inside Unity into a simple free-roam prototype. Existing asset packs could then cover less distinctive objects such as vehicles, street furniture and vegetation.

Cumbernauld is particularly suited to the idea because so much of its identity comes from the way the New Town was planned as a complete system rather than a conventional town that grew gradually. The original New Town was designated in 1956, with its roads, neighbourhoods, pedestrian routes and town centre shaped around a strongly planned post-war vision.

That physical environment is also entering a period of major real-world change. North Lanarkshire Council says the regeneration of The Centre Cumbernauld will involve its complete replacement over a long-term programme, with demolition expected to take around eight to 10 years. Current estimates put the first demolition stage in 2027-28 and the second in 2031-33.

That gives a digital recreation an extra archival dimension. A sufficiently detailed version could eventually preserve parts of the town as they existed before the next wave of redevelopment, while still functioning as a game rather than a heritage model.

No full development programme has been committed to and there is no finished prototype yet. The significance of the latest work is narrower: the project now has a plausible technical route, with the modelling work able to be done manually while Unity handles the explorable environment and AI can help bridge gaps in programming.

For an idea that once amounted to little more than wanting a hometown version of a favourite game, that is enough to move it from “wouldn’t it be good?” territory into something that could actually be built.

articles.title: Digital reset reaches public release
articles.standfirst: The public release of iOS 27 has caught up with SwS’s recent clean-install reset, moving the rebuilt Apple setup from release-candidate software onto the finished platform.

runs.text: Image: Apple’s iOS 27 and wider OS release. Source: Apple.
Digital reset reaches public release

SwS’s recent wholesale digital reset has reached its next stage after Apple released iOS 27 to the public, bringing the rebuilt personal setup onto the finished version of the software it was designed around.

The reset began before the general release, using the iOS 27, macOS 27 and watchOS 27 release candidates as the basis for a clean start across the main Apple devices. The iPhone and Mac were wiped, applications were reinstalled from scratch and the hardware itself was cleaned as part of a wider attempt to remove years of digital clutter.

Apple released iOS 27 on Monday 14 September, alongside its other major operating-system updates. The software brings the new Siri AI experience, further refinements to Liquid Glass and broader performance and search improvements. Apple says Siri AI can use personal context, work across apps and continue conversations through a dedicated Siri app.

For SwS, the timing means the reset is no longer sitting on pre-release software. The operating system around which the new setup was built has now become the standard public release, turning what began as an early clean-install exercise into the normal day-to-day configuration.

The bigger change remains organisational rather than cosmetic. Apple Photos has been reduced primarily to photographs captured on iPhone, while Google Photos is being used as the central home for the wider image archive, including older photographs, screenshots, textures and other visual material.

Google Drive has also been established as the main source of truth for projects and files, with Google Calendar taking over as the primary calendar. ChatGPT Projects are being used more deliberately for ongoing work, while Apollo Reborn has restored the preferred Reddit setup.

The approach is essentially a rejection of the usual upgrade cycle where new software is installed on top of an increasingly messy existing system. Instead, the September release became an excuse to reconsider what belongs on each device and which service should own each category of information.

There are practical benefits to doing that now. iOS 27’s improved system search and the new Siri AI both put greater emphasis on finding and acting on personal information. A cleaner division between photos, files, calendars and ongoing projects should make that information easier to manage even where Apple’s own intelligence features are not doing the work directly.

No further large-scale reset is planned. The focus now shifts from rebuilding the system to seeing whether the new structure survives ordinary use without gradually accumulating the same duplication and clutter it was designed to remove.
The software has changed overnight. The more interesting test is whether the habits change with it.

articles.title: One feed for SwS and the wider world
articles.standfirst: Work has begun on a new SWS.GOV Superfeed designed to mix Government for SwS updates with the wider news in one ranked stream.

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is moving towards a single news stream combining Government for SwS updates with stories from the wider world.
The plan is still at proposal stage, with implementation details and ranking weights yet to be settled.

The proposal would combine articles published through Craft with posts pulled from external RSS feeds. Instead of keeping personal publishing and outside news in separate lanes, the same ranking system would decide what appears prominently on the homepage and how the News section is ordered.
The idea is more ambitious than a simple chronological list.
SWS.GOV

material would receive a built-in advantage, reflecting the site’s role as the main record of SwS activity, but it would not automatically occupy every top slot. A sufficiently significant external story could rise above routine SwS updates.
That creates an unusual but useful editorial model: a personal website behaving more like a live news product, where a new
SWS.GOV
policy, project update or announcement can sit directly alongside major events in the wider world.
The proposal emerged during work on making better use of Codex with the
SWS.GOV

GitHub project. The immediate development brief is to build the feed as a reusable source rather than hard-wire it to one screen. That means the same ordered stream could power the homepage, become the default sorting method for News, or be called elsewhere in Project Indigo.
Craft is becoming more important to that system too.
SWS.GOV

’s publishing workflow is now moving towards the existing Articles collection in the Publisher space, with structured fields for status, section, tags and Superfeed behaviour. New fields include an importance setting and a pinned state, giving first-party articles explicit signals that can eventually feed into ranking.

For now, the default importance is Automatic. That leaves the system to make the normal ordering decision rather than requiring every article to be manually labelled Breaking, Major, Standard or Minor. Pinning is also off by default.
The key challenge is ranking without turning the feed into noise. Recency alone would be too crude: a minor
SWS.GOV
post published five minutes ago should not necessarily bury a genuinely major story. Equally, an external RSS source should not overwhelm the site simply because it publishes more frequently.

No final ranking formula has been implemented or announced. The current work is a product and engineering brief, and the precise weighting between source, recency, importance and other signals remains to be decided.
The direction is nevertheless clear. Project Indigo is moving away from a collection of separate content rows towards one editorial layer capable of answering a much simpler question: what should
SWS.GOV
show first right now?

Project Indigo now treats Google Docs as a structured article source, while Google Drive folders keep each publishing stream organised.
The publishing form creates the document, records its metadata and requests an immediate sync. Editors can then return to the Google Doc to refine the article.
This demonstration entry is part of the initial end-to-end test.

articles.title: SWS.GOV plans switch from Craft to Notion
articles.standfirst: A proposed change to article publishing would put Notion at the centre of editing while keeping the website independent of its API.

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is planning to move its article publishing system from Craft to Notion, in a proposed overhaul intended to make the site easier to maintain without introducing a paid content-management service.

The change is being considered as part of Project Indigo, the continuing rebuild of the Government for SwS website. Craft currently stores the official Articles collection, including News, Press Office and Daily Note content. It also provides the structured information used to decide which articles appear on the site and how they are presented.

Notion would take over as the place where articles are written, organised and prepared for publication. Its database system could manage titles, summaries, sections, tags, publishing dates and statuses, alongside the importance and pinning controls used by
SWS.GOV
's Superfeed.

The appeal is partly financial. Notion's Free plan offers unlimited pages and blocks for an individual workspace and access to its public API. That makes it a potential long-term home for a growing archive without a recurring subscription for the editorial software itself.

But the proposal is not simply to replace one API with another. Notion has request limits and its hosted media links can expire. Relying on live Notion requests every time someone opens an article would leave the website exposed to slow responses, temporary outages and unnecessary API traffic.
The preferred approach is to treat Notion as the editorial source while keeping a separate, persistent copy of published content for the website to serve. Changes would be synchronised into
SWS.GOV
, where articles could be validated, transformed into the site's existing content format and cached. Images would also need a dependable storage arrangement.
That separation matters as
SWS.GOV

develops its Superfeed. The system is designed to combine first-party Government for SwS news with stories from external RSS sources, applying editorial importance, recency and source signals to choose what appears most prominently. A change of writing software should not alter that ranking model or break established article links.
An inspection of the
SWS.GOV

GitHub repository found that the website already uses a dedicated article repository interface. The Superfeed obtains articles through that abstraction rather than depending directly on Craft. A Notion implementation could therefore reuse much of the existing presentation and ranking infrastructure.

Not everything is ready to switch. Craft-specific editing screens, publishing endpoints, image uploads and existing article conversion logic would still need to be adapted. Existing posts would have to be migrated and checked for formatting, images, dates and metadata, with their public URLs preserved.
The proposal also comes just after the introduction of a dedicated
SWS.GOV

News workflow inside ChatGPT. That workflow currently creates and verifies articles in Craft. If the migration proceeds, its publishing destination and verification steps would need to change as well.

No migration has yet been completed, and there is no confirmed launch date. The next stage would be to build and test a Notion article adapter, establish reliable synchronisation and then move the current archive before retiring Craft as the primary article source.
The wider aim is straightforward: keep editing convenient, publishing inexpensive and the website resilient, without allowing the choice of content editor to dictate the architecture of
SWS.GOV

articles.title: A newsroom inside ChatGPT
articles.standfirst: A new private SWS.GOV News plugin packages the editorial and publishing workflow for ChatGPT, with Craft verification built in.

runs.text: SWS.GOV
has acquired its own ChatGPT news-writing workflow after a private plugin was created on Wednesday 7 October, giving the site a reusable route from conversation to publication in Craft.
The plugin, named
SWS.GOV

News, was registered as a private version 0.1.0 release. Its job is to make a routine which previously required a long set of instructions available whenever a news story is needed. Rather than manually specifying the destination and fields each time, the editorial requirements now travel with the plugin.

The new workflow begins before a word is written. It asks ChatGPT to examine recent conversations across work, design, personal projects and everyday developments, then check the BBC calendar for relevant upcoming events. It must also inspect existing
SWS.GOV
articles to avoid recycling a story already published. A genuine follow-up needs a material new development; otherwise, no filler article should be produced.

Once a story is chosen, the brief calls for roughly 500 words of British-English reporting. Headlines must vary, and the writing should be brisk without tipping into parody. The rules prohibit invented quotes, officials, reactions or achievements. Proposals must remain proposals, not be presented as completed launches.

The destination is precise: the Articles collection in the Publisher space on Craft. Every new article starts as a Draft and carries its headline, unique slug, standfirst, publication date, News section, relevant tags and Craft source type. Superfeed importance is Automatic by default, and pinning stays off.

The crucial safeguard is verification. The article body and metadata must be read back before the status can change to Published. A second read confirms the final state. If an interrupted write leaves an incomplete item, the workflow is meant to repair that item instead of creating a duplicate.

The plugin follows an eventful first test of the direct Craft workflow. A Superfeed story was written and published on 7 October, although intermediate edits encountered tool-call restrictions before the full article could be verified. That experience exposed the value of keeping creation, writing and publication as separate checks.

There is an important limit. Creating the plugin establishes its reusable instructions; it does not by itself prove that every future Craft write will succeed. The plugin still depends on access to the relevant connected services, and its own end-to-end publishing behaviour remains to be tested.
For Project Indigo, the significance is practical.
SWS.GOV

already has a structured home for articles and an emerging Superfeed model for displaying them. A dedicated ChatGPT newsroom workflow is another attempt to reduce the work between spotting a worthwhile development and placing a properly checked report in the publishing system.
The newsroom has a new front door. The next test is whether it can use it reliably.

articles.title: GFT screenings set for SWS.GOV homepage
articles.standfirst: Plans for a live cinema carousel and listings page could later expand to Edinburgh Filmhouse.

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is planning to bring Glasgow Film Theatre screenings directly onto its homepage, with a new daily film carousel and a dedicated cinema listings page under consideration as part of Project Indigo.

The proposed feature, titled “Today at the GFT”, would display posters for films showing at the Glasgow cinema, with screening times listed beneath each title. Individual times would link to official booking pages, allowing the site to act as a straightforward guide to what is on without replacing the cinema’s own ticketing service.
The design brief calls for a deliberately minimal interface. Posters would sit in a horizontally scrolling row, using the established
SWS.GOV

typography, spacing and layout rather than introducing a separate cinema-themed design. On smaller screens the carousel would support touch gestures and show part of the next poster to indicate that more films are available. Subtle hover states, restrained transitions and keyboard navigation are also planned.

Films with several screenings on the same day would appear only once, with their times grouped together in chronological order. Screenings that have already passed would be subdued or removed so the component remains useful throughout the day. A separate listings page would offer a fuller programme, including date navigation and additional film information where available.
Finding a reliable source

The idea follows an investigation into Simple Cinema Listings, an independent website that presents GFT schedules in a stripped-back format. Its creator has previously described using Selenium browser automation to navigate the cinema website and collect listing links.

A more direct route may be possible. GFT’s website has previously exposed a GraphQL endpoint that could provide structured screening information without the need to automate clicks through the public interface. The endpoint and its current capabilities have not yet been verified, so the technical approach remains subject to investigation.
Under the proposed architecture,
SWS.GOV

would fetch and standardise cinema information on the server, cache it and make it available through an internal API. A refresh roughly every six hours is being considered, with the most recent successful data retained if the source temporarily becomes unavailable. The system would use UK local time and avoid displaying outdated screenings.
That separation would allow cinema data to be reused elsewhere in
SWS.GOV
, potentially including Planner or future recommendations features. Film showings would be handled as events rather than published news articles.
Edinburgh could follow
The plans are unlikely to stop at Glasgow.
Edinburgh Filmhouse is a likely candidate for inclusion in a future phase
, extending the listings beyond GFT and creating the possibility of a two-city independent cinema guide.

Simple Cinema Listings already demonstrates the appeal of presenting programming from both venues in a consistent format. However, Filmhouse would require its own investigation into available data sources, permissions and update reliability before an integration could be confirmed.
The proposal reflects a broader Project Indigo ambition to make
SWS.GOV

useful as a daily destination, combining personal publishing with practical information about life beyond the website. Cinema listings would offer a particularly tangible example: a simple glance at the homepage could reveal whether there is something worth seeing that evening.

No launch date has been confirmed, and neither cinema integration is yet live. The next step is to establish a reliable and appropriate source for GFT data, then implement and test the homepage component and wider listings interface.

articles.title: Pollok walk turns into a 10K
articles.standfirst: An after-work walk from the Southside into Pollok Country Park covered 9.83km, with more than two hours spent on foot.

runs.text: What started as a decision to get out after work turned into a substantial Southside walk on Wednesday, with a 9.83km route through Shawlands, Pollokshaws and Pollok Country Park.

The walk began at 16:09 and finished at 18:50, taking 2 hours 40 minutes from start to finish. Apple Watch recorded 2 hours 16 minutes of workout time, an average pace of 13 minutes 50 seconds per kilometre and 105 metres of elevation gain.

The route headed west from the Battlefield and Shawlands area, continued through Pollokshaws and entered Pollok Country Park before looping back east by a different route. Rather than treating the park as a single destination, the walk became a broad circuit through the Southside and the park landscape.

The original plan had been considerably less ambitious: an after-work visit to Pollok Country Park, with the possibility of a relatively short wander before heading home. In practice, the route grew into a little over six miles on foot.

The walk also provided an opportunity to pay closer attention to the changing urban landscape between Shawlands and Pollok. The route passes from dense tenement neighbourhoods and major roads into the older fabric of Pollokshaws, before crossing into the much greener and quieter park.

That contrast was part of the point. Recent Government for SwS thinking has put greater emphasis on spending time outdoors, moving around Glasgow on foot and engaging more deliberately with the Southside rather than defaulting to time at home after work.

The physical effort was significant without being a conventional high-intensity workout. Average heart rate was 125 bpm and the watch recorded 435 active calories, rising to 611 total calories over the session. The workout was rated at effort level 7, or Hard.

Heart rate remained relatively steady through the earlier kilometres before climbing later in the walk. The recorded graph shows a late peak of around 169 bpm. The first four kilometre splits were completed at between 11:46 and 12:41 per kilometre, before the pace slowed as the route continued.

The result is a useful addition to the normal Body routine. Walking does not replace the existing strength programme, but a long, low-intensity session can add meaningful movement and time outdoors without requiring another gym workout.

More importantly, it demonstrated that a weekday evening can accommodate something more substantial than the usual transition from work to home. Pollok Country Park is close enough to become part of normal Southside life rather than something reserved for a planned weekend trip.
The 9.83km circuit may have been more than intended, but that was ultimately the success of it: a spontaneous after-work walk became a proper Glasgow excursion.

articles.title: DIBI warning over culturally thin design
articles.standfirst: A standout Edinburgh conference talk challenges the idea that a single interface can work equally well across cultures.

blocks.alt: DIBI warning over culturally thin design

runs.text: A warning against culturally generic digital products has emerged as one of the strongest lessons from DIBI 2026, following a talk in Edinburgh on Thursday 1 October about what designers lose when they assume one interface can serve the whole world.

French designer Guillaume Valin examined how culture influences the way people interpret symbols, names, language and familiar digital conventions. The argument went beyond translating strings or swapping regional imagery. A product can be technically accessible and globally available while still making assumptions rooted in a narrow cultural context.

For SwS, whose work centres on UX design and experimentation, the session stood out among two days of presentations and workshops at DIBI. Its central lesson was that international design requires more than consistency. It demands attention to the meanings that different people attach to apparently universal interface elements.
The danger of a universal default

Valin drew attention to PlayStation controller symbols, phonetic name fields and changing interpretations of the @ symbol. These examples point to a recurring design problem: an element that seems obvious to one audience may carry a different association, or no useful association at all, for another.

Names are a particularly practical example. An interface built around a single set of assumptions about pronunciation, ordering or characters may work smoothly for its original audience but create unnecessary work elsewhere. Adding a translated label does not resolve a flawed underlying model.

The discussion also questioned whether redundancy in interfaces is always wasteful. Extra cues, labels or explanations can help establish meaning where a supposedly intuitive symbol does not travel well. Removing them in pursuit of visual simplicity may make a product cleaner for one group and less understandable for another.

Valin's suggested direction was a common product core supported by an adaptive layer, rather than either completely separate regional products or a rigid, one-size-fits-all interface. That distinction has direct implications for design systems: consistency should protect coherent behaviour, not freeze every cultural assumption into a universal component.
A question for AI design
The talk extended the issue to AI, raising the possibility that systems trained and deployed at enormous scale could flatten cultural differences rather than reflect them.

The risk is not necessarily an obviously incorrect answer or interface. It is something subtler: outputs that feel broadly acceptable but lack the local voice, context and distinctions that give communication meaning. Valin described the result as culturally thin.

The observation adds nuance to the wider AI debate heard at DIBI. Other sessions focused on the growing influence of AI in products and workplaces, including the relationship between AI systems and established software tools. Valin's contribution asked a different question: what qualities should technological progress preserve?

For Government for SwS, the practical response is to treat cultural assumptions as design decisions that can be identified, tested and reconsidered. That applies to forms, terminology, icons, content and the increasingly common use of generative AI in design workflows.
Beyond the conference

DIBI took place across 30 September and 1 October, with workshops and talks covering storytelling, coding, product development and artificial intelligence. The cultural design session became a personal highlight, offering a particularly useful counterweight to claims that AI and global design systems naturally make digital work more universal.
Its lesson is straightforward but demanding. A product does not become inclusive simply because it can be used everywhere. Designers must understand what changes when it arrives somewhere new.
The challenge is not to abandon shared standards. It is to make sure that shared standards leave room for difference.
